  • A sandbox such as Flatpak connects its apps through a socket of wp-security-context-v1. Those clients do not see the privileged protocols: the layer shell, the session lock, the input method, both foreign toplevel protocols, output management, both screencopy protocols with their sources, and the security context manager itself.
  • The IPC methods input.inject and screen.capture need a grant of the user for the client name: choractl grant NAME CAPABILITY. A grant protects against mistakes of agents. It is no barrier against hostile code of the same user. The emergency reset revokes all grants.
  • screen.capture and input.inject fail while the session is locked.
  • The core starts no program except its own startup command (D42). choractl run starts programs outside it, and systemd units keep plugins running.
  • A connection of a client socket acts only on its own nodes and on the windows of its wayland.sock. It sets no camera and puts no node under screen:*. It takes the keyboard with focus_node or focus only after a press of the user on it (see API).

docs.title: Sessions and flavors
docs.text: A login session runs chora as a systemd user unit, through uwsm or through chora-session, and chora starts the systemd target of a flavor. See Sessions and Flavors.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Views are YAML files in git, and an agent can read and write them. A strict schema validates each file. It rejects unknown keys and catches the YAML traps, for example no read as false.

The core reads no configuration file. It runs one startup command (D30), for example chora-flavor, which starts the systemd target of a flavor:

chora -- chora-flavor tiling

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
~/.config/chora/
├── views/              # one file per view
├── flavors/            # bundles of views, plugins and services
├── plugins/            # plugin manifests
├── shaders/            # GLSL ES shaders
├── clients.yaml        # the names and capabilities of `clients up`
└── chora-tiling.yaml   # the options and bindings of chora-tiling

The directory is a git repository. It contains no secrets. The package installs the reference flavors to /usr/share/chora/.

Fonts are not there: the core draws text with the system fonts and with every directory listed in CHORA_FONT_DIRS, separated by :. A user font in ~/.local/share/fonts needs no setting at all.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
A view is a part of the scene and the plugins that drive it (D35):

# ~/.config/chora/views/work.yaml
name: work
plugins:
- name: tiling
  config: {layout: fair, gap: 12}
scene:
- id: work-corner
  kind: group
  props:
    transform: {translate: [1800, 20]}
- id: work-badge
  kind: rect
  parent: work-corner
  props:
    size: [100, 30]
    color: [0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0]
input:
  keyboard: {repeat_rate: 30, repeat_delay: 250}
  touchpad: {tap: true, natural_scroll: true}
  mouse: {accel_profile: flat, accel_speed: -0.2}
  • choractl view load work first sends input to the core method input.configure, if the view has it. Then it starts each plugin of the view that does not run yet, with the exec of its manifest. It waits up to 10 s until the plugin connects. It passes each config to the method that the manifest names in configure. Then it applies the nodes of the view as one transaction. It prints the started plugins, the count of nodes and, as input, the answer of input.configure.
  • The client view-work owns the nodes. A second load replaces them, choractl view unload work removes them.
  • choractl view save work writes the nodes of view-work as they are now to ~/.config/chora/views/work.yaml, or to --file PATH. It keeps the plugins and the input of the file that was there, not the live settings of the core. A plugin or an agent changes the nodes as view-work, for example choractl --name view-work apply.
  • A node has an id, a kind (group, rect, image, shader or text), a parent (the root by default) and its props as in a create command.
  • A name has lowercase letters, digits, _, - and ., and starts with a letter, so that its file stays in its directory. A name does not end in .yaml, because such a name is a path. The file NAME.yaml must name the same view.
  • choractl view load also takes the path of a YAML file; the MCP tools take names only.
  • input sets the input devices of the whole session through input.configure, so the core reads no file for them (D35). keyboard has repeat_rate and repeat_delay. touchpad and mouse have tap, natural_scroll, left_handed, accel_profile and accel_speed. IPC methods gives the ranges and the rules.
  • A plugin that a view starts gets no stdin and no stdout of choractl, which carry MCP under choractl mcp.

choractl looks for NAME.yaml in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/chora/views/ first (~/.config/chora/views/ by default), and then in /usr/share/chora/views/.

docs.title: Strict YAML
docs.text: choractl reads views and manifests with serde-saphyr (D41). Unknown keys, duplicate keys and unknown tags are errors. Only true and false are booleans, so no stays the string no.

docs.title: Plugin manifests
docs.text:
A manifest tells choractl how to start and how to configure a plugin. It lives in plugins/NAME.yaml of the same directories:

# /usr/share/chora/plugins/tiling.yaml
name: tiling
exec: chora-tiling
configure: set_layout
description: Tiles the windows with the tags and layouts of awesome.
Key Meaning name the client name of the plugin exec the shell command that starts it configure the exported method that takes the config of a view; a view without config needs none description what the plugin does

The package installs the manifest of chora-tiling.

docs.title: Clients file
docs.text:
choractl clients up [FILE] applies a file that maps client names to their grants (see API):

# ~/.config/chora/clients.yaml
agent:
  grants: [screen.capture]
showroom:
  grants: []

The grants are the seven capabilities of choractl grant (see API). An agent that drives the window manager needs methods.call, and one that starts apps needs activation.token. Both let it take the keyboard focus. A name that may end chora needs session.quit. A name that may change the settings of a plugin, or call a plugin method that starts programs, such as app.open of chora-mc, also needs methods.privileged. So does a name that sets the input devices with input.configure.

The names follow the rules of hello. clients up opens the socket of every name with exactly the capabilities of its list. A socket that already has the equal capabilities stays with its connections and gets them back after the revoke binding. Changed capabilities recreate the socket and disconnect its Wayland clients. A name with a client socket takes no choractl grant and no choractl revoke; the file decides. While a name is connected, its socket cannot open. clients up then only syncs the grants of the name and says on stderr that the socket stays closed.

docs.title: chora-tiling
docs.text:
chora-tiling connects with the client name tiling. Grants and choractl restart use this name.

Flag Meaning --config FILE the settings file instead of $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/chora/chora-tiling.yaml --print-config prints the default settings and exits --output NAME manages only this output; can come more than once (see below) --ignore APP_ID leaves the windows with this app id to other clients; can come more than once

chora-tiling reads chora/chora-tiling.yaml in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME, by default ~/.config, or the file of --config. Without a file, it uses its default, which chora-tiling --print-config prints. The file holds the settings of D62: settings.set changes them at once and writes the file again, without its comments (see API). Edits by hand apply with settings.reload or MOD+Ctrl+r, or at the next start of the plugin. The default file lists every option. A file can leave options out, and they take their defaults; a map such as bindings in the file replaces the default map:

Option Meaning modifier what MOD means in the bindings: Super or Alt gap the gap around each window, in logical pixels tags the number of tags of each output, at most 16 layouts the layouts in the order of next_layout; each tag starts with the first master_width, masters, columns the start values of each tag for the tile layouts new_window master or stack: where a new window goes focus click or follow_mouse style how a new window looks: opacity from 0 to 1, and effects, a list of shaders as in scene.apply (#99); chora-tiling sets it once, when it takes the window; a look that another client asks for wins (see below) bindings a binding with MOD, and its action; the default file uses every action at least once; run: CMD starts a shell command with choractl run

The layouts and the default bindings follow the awesome window manager. Each output has its own tags, and each tag its own layout and parameters. A window can be on several tags, and an output can show several tags. A floating, maximized or fullscreen window leaves the tiles. A click or a binding raises the window that it focuses; the focus that follows the pointer raises nothing. The binding MOD+Ctrl+r reads the file again. Mouse moves and resizes of floating windows do not exist.

chora-tiling exports methods for other clients (see Plugin methods). Every method but get_layout and get_tags changes something and answers with the layout info of the current tag, like set_layout. The gap of set_layout is a live value: the file keeps the old gap, and the next settings.set or settings.reload sets the gap of the file again.

Method Parameters Does the same as set_layout, get_layout see API the layout of the current tag get_tags none, see API the tags of each output, for a panel give to: a client name handing the focused window to another client view_tag tag: a tag number MOD+1 to MOD+9 move_to_tag surface, tag MOD+Shift+1 to MOD+Shift+9, for this window focus surface a click: focuses and raises the window, and its output; a window that shows nowhere only gets the urgent mark focus_next, focus_prev none MOD+j and MOD+k swap_master surface MOD+Ctrl+Return, for this window settings.get, settings.set, settings.reload see API an edit of the file and MOD+Ctrl+r

chora-tiling connects with resume (see API). It keeps the tags and the layouts of each output, and the tags, the states and the stacking of each window, in the meta of its nodes. A restart within the grace time rebuilds them from there. In a flavor or a view, choractl restart tiling does that after a rebuild.

Another client changes the opacity, the effects or the meta of a tiling window with an update of the window (D58). The core asks chora-tiling with node.requested, and chora-tiling applies it, except the meta key window, which holds its own state. A layout or a tag never changes the opacity or the effects, so the requested look stays across relayouts, layout changes, tag moves and restarts with resume. The style applies only when chora-tiling takes a new window, so a requested value wins over the style for that window.

chora-tiling claims the box around the work areas of its outputs (D55). --output NAME limits it to some outputs, as for chora-xp, and can come more than once. So each window manager takes its own outputs. It leaves a new window that the core reserves for another client to that client. When the last of its --output outputs goes, it gives its windows away, and another window manager adopts them. It takes new windows again when one of its outputs comes back. Next to chora-xp, tiling needs modifier: Super: with Alt, tiling grabs Alt+Space for next_layout, and the system menu of XP does not open.

docs.title: chora-mc (experimental)
docs.text:
Experimental

chora-mc is an experiment. It is not in the packages, and its methods and files change without notice.

chora-mc connects with the client name mc. It is a voice-first desktop without window management: the whole screen shows one scene at a time on the first output, and quiet regions around it show the context: the running head and the clock, what the voice agent does, notes and a docked terminal. The voice agent and small collector scripts fill the scenes through methods; the plugin reads no sources itself.

A scene of chora-mc is not a view of D35. It is a YAML file NAME.yaml in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/chora/mc/scenes/: a grid of panels, each with a title and lines, or one app whose window fills the screen without a frame. The plugin has the built-in scenes agenda, agents, mission (Mission Control), morning (the morning paper) and terminal. A file of the same name replaces a built-in scene. A grid has 1 to 24 columns and rows. A wrong file, or a scene that the core refuses, is left out with a line in the log; the other scenes stay.

# ~/.config/chora/mc/scenes/day.yaml
grid: [2, 2]          # columns and rows
chapter:              # all optional: the place, the name, the date
  number: "2"
  title: Day
  running_head: Week 44
panels:
- id: mail
  cell: [0, 0, 1, 1]  # column, row, width and height in cells
  title: Mail
  style: {base: body, color: accent}   # a style of the settings, changed
- id: agents
  cell: [1, 0, 1, 2]
  title: Agents

Each scene of panels has a head in the style of the LaTeX package classicthesis: the running head in the header (see the regions below), and the number and the title of the scene as chapter.layout sets. The panels share the text block, one column of page.measure per column of the grid. A line TIME<tab>TEXT puts the time in the margin column left of the text, flush right, and the text wraps under it. A panel names the styles of its lines, its title and its notes with style, title_style and note_style; each takes a base (by default body, heading and margin) and changes single fields.

A scene may set its own page (measure, margin and gap, as in the settings), for example narrow columns side by side on a wide screen, and chapter.layout, also none for a scene without a head. Columns of a grid leave room for the margin of the column to their right. A panel may set a rule, a color of the theme for a hairline left of it, an opacity from 0 to 1 and a blur radius in pixels up to 16, for context that steps back (plugins/chora-mc/blur.frag).

The methods marked privileged start programs: a caller on a client socket needs methods.privileged besides methods.call.

mc also follows the events of the voice agent (D65); it subscribes to voice.*. voice.state sets the agent voice as agent.set does, or the sub-agent that the name of its data names, such as coder. voice.say shows a sentence as hud.say does. Data that mc does not take only goes to its log, since the emitter gets no answer. Other clients use agent.set and hud.say.

Method Parameters scene.show name; the scene fades in, the old one fades out scene.list none; answers scenes and current scene.save privileged. name, grid, panels or app; writes the file panel.set scene, panel, lines and an optional title; until the next start. A line with a tab puts the part before the first tab in the margin hud.set state, for example listening, thinking or working, and text; both empty hide the line. The line shows the last 160 characters of the text, from a word on hud.say text, duration_ms and an optional state: the text shows word by word over the duration, the time that the voice takes to speak it; past 160 characters the first words leave the line app.open privileged. command: a shell command that starts in a scene of its own region.list none; answers the current scene, each region with shown, visible and its contents, and each content with its kind, title, text and whether its app runs region.toggle privileged, because a docked app starts. region and an optional shown; without it the region flips. Answers shown region.put privileged. content, region and an optional slot: the content goes there over the rules, until the next start. Without region the content follows the rules again content.set content, lines and an optional title of a text content content.add content and line: adds a line to a text content, such as a note; the oldest go after 12 lines region.solo privileged. content, region and an optional shown: the content shows alone in the region over any scene, such as the test overlay in the drawer; without shown it flips. Hidden again, the region shows as before. Answers shown agent.set name and optional state, task, said and voice: adds an agent or changes it; a missing field stays. The state is a name of states agent.remove name agent.list none; answers agents, each with name, state, task, said, voice and since (the time of its first report) notify.push title, an optional body and an optional urgency (low, normal or critical): the line HH:MM title: body goes on top of the text notify; a critical one also shows in red in the text urgent until the next one notify.clear none; empties notify and urgent

New text writes itself, as Write of manim: a soft front draws the outlines line by line, and the fill follows. This happens when a scene shows and when panel.set changes the text of a panel; the same text again changes nothing. The effect is plugins/chora-mc/write.frag, and the animate of the core moves its uniform progress from 0 to 1.

A window that no scene started, for example from a launcher, gets a scene of its own. The settings of D62 are in chora/chora-mc.yaml; edits by hand apply with settings.reload:

  • theme (light or dark) and the colors of each theme by name, at least a background.
  • scale: the font sizes as steps of a modular scale (base, ratio), and the baseline grid; each line of text is whole lines of the grid.
  • styles: named styles with base, family, weight, style (normal or italic), size or step, color (a name of the theme or RGBA), line_height, letter_spacing in em, OpenType features and uppercase. The plugin uses chapter_number, chapter, chapter_large, running_head, heading, body, margin and hud. The default sets TeX Gyre Pagella with small caps and old-style figures for the text, from the Fedora package texlive-tex-gyre, whose directory /usr/share/texlive/texmf-dist/fonts/opentype/public/tex-gyre must be in CHORA_FONT_DIRS, and Inter with tabular figures for the running head, the notes and the HUD.
  • chapter.layout: number (a large light number, the title in spaced small caps below), caps (the title only), large (one large light title) or none.
  • page: the measure of a column of text, the margin column and the gap, in em of scale.base.
  • write: enabled (default true) and duration_ms (default 900).
  • default_scene, and the bindings with the actions next_scene, previous_scene, scene: NAME, run: COMMAND, toggle: REGION and solo: {content: NAME, region: REGION} (as region.solo; the default Super+F12 shows the test overlay in the drawer).
  • states: the states of agent.set, each with a sign, a color of the theme and an optional label for the agents scene. The default has idle ○, listening ◉, thinking ◌, working ●, speaking ◐, question ? (has a question), blocked ✕, done ✓ and asleep ☾: blue hears or thinks, green works or is done, the accent speaks, amber needs you, red is blocked, faint rests. The themes have the colors green, amber, blue and red for them.
  • regions, contents, rules, preset and presets: see below.

docs.title: Regions
docs.text:
The regions around the page follow the Emacs package auto-side-windows: rules put each content into a region and a slot, and a key shows or hides a region. The page itself never moves when a region shows.

 ______________________________________________________
|  header:  1  AGENDA       LISTENING   FRIDAY 16:08   |
|        |                                  |          |
|  left  |  margin   the page of the scene  |  right:  |
|        |                                  |  NOTES   |
|      __|__________________________________|__        |
|     |  drawer: a docked terminal (foot)     |       |
|     |_______________________________________|       |
|  footer:  words of the agent          15:15 Call    |
|______________________________________________________|
  • header and footer are lines over and under the text block, each size lines of the baseline grid high. Their contents stand side by side: a slot below 0 goes left, 0 in the middle, above 0 right. The right end keeps its place, the left end comes next, and a text that does not fit ends in an ellipsis.
  • left and right are columns beside the page, size em wide, their contents one under the other with a title in the style running_head. The page leaves room for a side that has contents, so that its text never moves; where both sides would leave the text less than three quarters of its measure, the sides do not show.
  • drawer is a sheet of size lines over the bottom of the page, with a hairline above it, for a docked app.

A region shows only with something in it. Whether it shows comes from a toggle, else from the regions of the scene file (for example regions: {right: false}), else from the preset, else from shown in regions. Over an app, the left and the right side show only after a toggle, and the app window leaves the header, the footer, the drawer and a shown side free. A toggle stays for all scenes.

The contents are named. Their kind is one of:

Kind Shows head the running head of the scene: chapter.running_head, else its number and title; the name of an app clock the time as date formats it with format, each minute anew state the state of hud.set and hud.say, in the accent color hud the text of hud.set and hud.say agents the sign and the name of each agent of agent.set, each in the color of its state, in the style hud text a title and lines that content.set and content.add change app a docked command; {NAME} in it is the color NAME of the theme as RRGGBB

Each content may set a style. The rules are a list, and the first rule that matches a content wins. A rule names a content or a kind, optionally the scenes by name or @app and @page, and the region and slot. A rule cannot put an app into a line.

toggle: REGION as a binding shows or hides a region. A region with a docked app works as a quake terminal: the first press starts the app and gives it the keyboard, a press while the app has no keyboard gives it back to it, and the next press hides the region and gives the keyboard back to the scene. When the app ends, its region hides. A drawer that a preset or a scene shows starts its app when the settings load.

The default bindings are Super+Return for the drawer, Super+n for the right side, and Super+Up and Super+Down for the header and the footer.

The default desk setup: the header shows the running head left, and the agents, the state of the agent and the clock right; the footer shows the words of the agent left, a critical notification in red in the middle and the next entry of the agenda right (the collector fills the content next); the right side shows the notes, which an agent fills with content.add, and the notifications below them, newest on top; Super+Return opens foot in the drawer in the colors of the theme. Over an app, the words of the agent move into the middle of the header. On a narrow page the header has no room for many agents and the long clock: the end of the line is cut. Set the rule of time instead of clock there.

preset picks an arrangement of presets. A preset sets which regions show in shown and has its own rules; without rules, those of the settings apply:

Preset Arrangement quiet only the header: the running head, the words and the state of the agent, the time desk the default described above studio an outline and the notes in the left side, a terminal in the drawer that starts at once book the running head and the date above, the words of the agent, the time as a folio and the state below, the notes in the margin 
# ~/.config/chora/chora-mc.yaml
preset: desk              # desk has no rules of its own
contents:
  todo: {kind: text, title: Today}
rules:                    # the list replaces the default rules
- {content: head, region: header, slot: -1}
- {content: clock, region: header, slot: 1}
- {content: hud, region: footer, slot: -1}
- {content: todo, scenes: ['@page'], region: left}
- {content: notes, region: right}
- {kind: app, region: drawer}

choractl call mc content.add '{"content": "notes", "line": "Call Lena"}'
choractl call mc region.toggle '{"region": "drawer"}'
choractl call mc region.put '{"content": "notes", "region": "left"}'

chora-mc --print-config prints the default. An option that the file leaves out takes its default. The collector plugins/chora-mc/collectors/agenda.sh puts the org agenda of today into the scene agenda, with emacs --batch: the entries with a time, and the tasks scheduled or due today, each as a time in the margin and a text. It leaves out overdue, upcoming and done tasks. ORG_TODO sets the TODO keywords, by default PROJ TODO NEXT WAIT | DONE KILL.

The other collectors in plugins/chora-mc/collectors/ are Python 3 scripts without dependencies. They only read their sources, and a source that is missing leaves a short note or nothing. Each takes --print to show the JSON without chora:

Collector Fills Sources morning.py [ORG_FILE...] the scene morning: the lead (the first task due today, else the next entry), the weather, the day, the mail, overnight and the reading list agenda.sh; wttr.in for the place MC_WEATHER (by IP without it), cached for an hour in $XDG_CACHE_HOME/chora-mc, nothing when offline; notmuch (unread mail in the inbox), a hint without it; the agents of agent.list that are done, nothing without them; the reading list MC_READING (default ~/Notes/reading.md): items of markdown or org, the done ones left out system.py [--every S] [--once] the scene mission, every 5 seconds: load with a cpu sparkline of the last 24 rounds, the busy processes, the errors of the journal today, the failed units, host facts /proc/stat, /proc/meminfo, /proc/net/dev, /sys/class/thermal, ps; once a minute journalctl -p err -b --since today -o json, systemctl --failed and systemctl --user --failed tests.py [--every S] the text overlay, the test sheet of Super+F12 gh run list in MC_REPO (the repository of the script by default); gate results in MC_GATES (default MC_REPO/target/gates), one file per gate whose last ok:, SKIP: or FAIL: line counts; choractl query '*' for the nodes by owner; the memory of the chora processes

Run morning.py from a timer in the morning, and system.py while the session runs, for example as a user unit. The agents scene needs no collector: agent.set and the event voice.state fill the panel agent-N with the N-th agent (its title in the color of its state, the sign and the state, its task and its last words) and band-N below it with its voice and its start; a scene file with more columns shows more agents.

choractl call mc agent.set '{"name": "coder", "state": "working", "task": "Runs the tests"}'
choractl call mc notify.push '{"title": "CI", "body": "dev failed", "urgency": "critical"}'
choractl call mc region.solo '{"content": "overlay", "region": "drawer"}'

docs.title: Flavors
docs.text: A flavor is a directory with views, plugin manifests and services, plus a systemd user target chora-<name>.target. chora-flavor <name> looks for the directory in ~/.config/chora/flavors/ first and then in /usr/share/chora/flavors/. It imports WAYLAND_DISPLAY, CHORA_SOCKET, CHORA_FLAVOR_DIR (the directory that it found) and the X11 DISPLAY of xwayland-satellite into the systemd user manager. So every unit of the flavor starts with them. It links the units of the directory, tells systemd that chora is ready, and starts the target. The target starts the services and the plugins. systemd handles start, restart and order, so chora needs no service manager. chora-flavor is not for nested use: its variables would reach the units of the host session.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
The login screen shows a session per flavor, twice:

Session Starts chora (uwsm), chora (Windows XP, uwsm) uwsm start -e -D chora -N chora -- chora -- chora-flavor <name> (D50) chora, chora (Windows XP) chora-session <name>, without uwsm

The uwsm sessions show only when uwsm is installed. uwsm is not in Fedora 44, so there the sessions without uwsm are the fallback (D50). uwsm runs chora as the user unit wayland-wm@chora.service and binds it to graphical-session.target. Under uwsm, chora-flavor calls uwsm finalize with its variables: uwsm exports them, marks chora as ready and removes the variables again when the session ends. Before chora starts, uwsm sources /etc/xdg/uwsm/env-chora. Without XKB_DEFAULT_LAYOUT, this file takes the keyboard layout of the system from localectl. ~/.config/uwsm/env-chora adds variables of the user.

chora-session does the same without uwsm. It sources /etc/xdg/uwsm/env-chora, imports the environment of the login into the systemd user manager and runs chora as chora@<name>.service. The unit drops a WAYLAND_DISPLAY and a DISPLAY that another session left in the user manager, because chora would then run nested. When chora ends, chora-session stops the units of the graphical session.

docs.title: Screen sharing
docs.text:
Browsers and video calls share the screen through xdg-desktop-portal, which hands the work to xdg-desktop-portal-wlr (D37). Both sessions set XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP=chora, and chora-flavor gives it and WAYLAND_DISPLAY to systemd and D-Bus, so that the portals start with them. chora-flavor also stops a portal that an earlier session in the same user manager started. The next call starts it again with the variables of chora. While another graphical session of the user is open, the portal stays. The packages install two files:

  • /usr/share/xdg-desktop-portal/chora-portals.conf: for XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP=chora, screen sharing and screenshots go through xdg-desktop-portal-wlr, the other portals through xdg-desktop-portal-gtk.
  • /etc/xdg/xdg-desktop-portal-wlr/chora: fuzzel asks which output or window to share. ~/.config/xdg-desktop-portal-wlr/chora replaces it, for example with chooser_type=none and output_name=eDP-1 to share that output without a question.

xdg-desktop-portal-wlr captures through ext-image-copy-capture, and through wlr-screencopy on older versions. It shares outputs, and windows of ext-foreign-toplevel-list. The core copies through shm, so each frame takes a copy on the CPU, and the shared picture has no cursor. The portal runs on the Wayland socket of the session, which has every capture protocol. A client of a client socket needs the grant screen.capture (see API).

docs.title: X11 programs
docs.text: xwayland-satellite runs X11 programs as Wayland windows. When it is installed, chora-flavor picks a free display, for example :0, and gives DISPLAY to systemd and D-Bus. The unit chora-<flavor>-xwayland.service of each flavor then starts xwayland-satellite on this display. The X11 windows are toplevels like all others, so chora-tiling tiles them.

docs.title: The tiling flavor
docs.text:
The package installs the tiling flavor (D51):

/usr/share/chora/flavors/tiling/
├── chora-tiling.target               # wants the units below and mako.service
├── chora-tiling.service              # chora-tiling
├── chora-tiling-xwayland.service     # xwayland-satellite
├── chora-tiling-waybar.service       # the panel
├── chora-tiling-swaybg.service       # the wallpaper, a plain color
├── chora-tiling-swayidle.service     # the idle lock with swaylock
├── chora-tiling-kanshi.service       # the output profiles of the user
└── waybar/
    ├── config.jsonc                  # the modules of the panel
    └── tags.jq                       # the text of the tags module

Each unit starts only when its program is installed. The packages recommend them: uwsm, foot, fuzzel, waybar, jq, mako, swaybg, swayidle, swaylock, kanshi, xwayland-satellite, xdg-desktop-portal-wlr and xdg-desktop-portal-gtk. mako starts from the unit of its own package and needs no configuration.

  • The panel: waybar with the configuration of the flavor. It shows only modules that need no IPC of sway: the tags of the output, the layout of the current tag, the clock, the volume, the network, the processor, the memory, the battery and the tray. The layout module calls choractl call tiling get_layout each second. The tags module calls choractl call tiling get_tags each second, and jq with waybar/tags.jq turns the answer into the text: the shown and the occupied tags, shown ones underlined, focused ones bold and urgent ones red.
  • The launcher: MOD+r starts fuzzel, as the default bindings of chora-tiling say.
  • The lock: swayidle runs swaylock -f after 5 minutes without input, before sleep, and on loginctl lock-session, which MOD+Shift+Escape runs. swaylock locks through the session lock protocol of the core. The core has no protocol to turn outputs off yet, so the screens stay on.
  • The wallpaper: swaybg with a plain color. For a picture, override the command:
systemctl --user edit chora-tiling-swaybg.service
# [Service]
# ExecStart=
# ExecStart=/usr/bin/swaybg --image %h/Pictures/wall.png --mode fill
  • The outputs: kanshi starts only when ~/.config/kanshi/config exists, because it fails without profiles. The core takes the configuration through wlr-output-management. An example with the names that wlr-randr prints:
profile docked {
  output eDP-1 disable
  output "Dell Inc. DELL U2720Q *" mode 3840x2160 scale 1.5
}
profile mobile {
  output eDP-1 enable scale 1.25
}

A copy of the directory in ~/.config/chora/flavors/tiling/ replaces it, also the configuration of waybar. systemctl --user edit UNIT changes a single unit. A user who enabled waybar.service of the waybar package gets a second panel; systemctl --user disable waybar.service ends it.

docs.title: The XP flavor
docs.text:
The XP flavor is the showroom (D39): a stacking desktop in the style of Windows XP. It is a demo, not a daily driver. chora-xp connects with the client name xp.

/usr/share/chora/flavors/xp/
├── chora-xp.target              # wants the two units below
├── chora-xp.service             # chora-xp
├── chora-xp-xwayland.service    # xwayland-satellite, if installed
└── theme/                       # SVG files, fonts, wallpaper and cursors

The session "chora (Windows XP)" on the login screen starts it with the XP cursors, which the package installs to /usr/share/icons/ModernXP. theme/README.md lists the source and the license of every file of the theme.

When the files of Windows XP are installed in the XDG data directory, as get-microsoft-files.sh of kde-plasma-winxp-launcher does, chora-xp uses them instead of the free files of the theme:

  • fonts/WindowsXP/: XP's Tahoma for the text, Trebuchet MS Bold for the titles and Franklin Gothic Medium Italic for the start button. These fonts go before the system fonts, so XP's Tahoma wins over the Tahoma of newer Windows.
  • wallpapers/WindowsXP/*.jpg: Bliss (bliss.jpg) is the wallpaper instead of Bløff, and Control Panel > Desktop lists all of them.
  • winxp-kde/start_flag.png: XP's flag on the start button, at its own size of 20 pixels.
  • sounds/WindowsXP/stereo/: XP's sounds. login.wav plays when chora-xp starts, logout.wav on Log Off, shutdown.wav on Turn Off and notify.wav when a balloon opens. The first of pw-play, paplay and canberra-gtk-play on the PATH plays them in the background.

The Luna GTK theme and the icons of xfce-winxp-tc give GTK applications, such as the file manager, an XP look. They hold non-free files of Windows XP: the user installs them, and chora does not ship them.

chora-xp draws everything as image nodes. It rasterizes the SVG files of the theme with resvg into PNG files in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/chora-xp/. It renders each picture once, at the largest scale of the outputs, but at most 4. Thus text and icons stay sharp on a scaled output. After a change of the scale, it renders the pictures again. The borders of windows and dialogs and the background of the taskbar stay at scale 1. The core reads the insets of a slice in pixels of the file. The pictures:

  • a frame around each window, with its title and the minimize, maximize and close buttons; a window that draws its own frame, as GTK programs do, gets none;
  • a taskbar at the bottom of the work area of each output, with the start button, one button per window of the current desktop, four desktop buttons and a clock;
  • the start menu with the user name, programs, places, the Control Panel, Log Off and Turn Off Computer, and All Programs with the applications of the desktop files in $XDG_DATA_HOME/applications and $XDG_DATA_DIRS, in program groups by their main category;
  • the icons of the desktop, between the wallpaper and the windows;
  • the wallpaper below everything: Bliss when it is installed, else Bløff.

A click on a window raises and focuses it. A drag of a title bar moves the window, and a double click maximizes it. chora-xp claims the box around the work areas of its outputs (D55). --output NAME limits it to some outputs. A window dragged out of these work areas goes to the window manager tiling with remove and to. Without tiling, the window stays. A drag of the border of the frame resizes the window: the 4 pixel border and 6 pixels of the shadow outside it take the press, and the corners reach 16 pixels along both edges. The client gets the new size once per frame while the button is down, and the edges that the drag does not move stay in place. A window is at least 112 by 35 pixels with its frame, so that the buttons of the title bar fit. A window that draws its own frame resizes from a strip of 6 pixels around it. A maximized window does not resize, and a window does not wobble while it resizes. The pointer keeps its arrow over the border: plugins cannot set the cursor. The core reports no size limits of a client yet, so a client that wants another size than it gets simply takes its own, and the frame follows it.

A right click on a title bar, a click on the icon of a title bar and a right click on a task button open XP's system menu, in the look of the context menus below: Restore, Move, Size, Minimize, Maximize and Close in bold with Alt+F4, with XP's glyphs. Restore is gray unless the window is maximized or minimized, Minimize is gray for a minimized window and Maximize for a maximized one. Move and Size are always gray: chora-xp moves and sizes windows with the mouse, and does not have XP's keyboard commands for them. The click on the icon opens the menu below the icon, the others at the pointer. A double click on the icon closes the window, as on XP. A maximized window fills the work area above the taskbar. When an output changes, for example its mode or its scale, its shown windows move back into its work area. A window that does not fit shrinks to it. A click on a task button shows or minimizes its window. Buttons light up under the pointer, and so do the entries of the start menu. All Programs and its groups open their cascading menus when the pointer rests on them for 350 ms, or on a click. A click on a program starts it and closes the menu; a click outside closes the menu. The open menu takes the keyboard. Up and Down move in a column or a cascade. Left and Right go between the columns and into and out of the cascades. Return starts the entry. Escape closes the innermost cascade, then the menu.

chora-xp draws no programs into the scene except the dialogs of the XP shell (D63): Log Off, Turn Off, Display Properties, Taskbar and Start Menu Properties, Date and Time Properties and the Control Panel menu. Folders open in the file manager of the setting file_manager, thunar by default: My Documents, My Pictures and My Music of the start menu (XDG_DOCUMENTS_DIR, XDG_PICTURES_DIR and XDG_MUSIC_DIR, else the home directory and its folders Pictures and Music), and My Computer as /. chora-xp adds the folder to the command, for example thunar '/home/user/Music'.

The desktop of the first output shows XP's icons in its grid of 75 by 75 pixels: My Documents (XDG_DOCUMENTS_DIR, else the home directory) and My Computer at the top left, then the folders and files of the Desktop folder (XDG_DESKTOP_DIR, else ~/Desktop) by name, folders first, in columns from the top. The Recycle Bin sits at the bottom right and shows whether $XDG_DATA_HOME/Trash/files has files. A desktop file shows its name and icon. A program, a desktop file or a window without an icon gets XP's icon of a program, application-x-executable of the icon theme. Each label is Tahoma in white with a black shadow, in at most two lines. chora-xp looks at the Desktop folder and the trash once a second. The icons that stay keep their cells. A new icon takes the first free cell of the columns. My Network Places is left out, because without a network browser it opens nothing.

A click selects an icon: its label turns white on dark blue, with a dotted focus rectangle while no window has the focus. A click on the empty desktop takes the selection away. A double click opens the icon. A folder and My Documents open in the file manager, My Computer opens / and the Recycle Bin opens $XDG_DATA_HOME/Trash/files in it. A desktop file runs its program, and any other file opens with xdg-open. A drag moves an icon to the nearest free cell of the grid, until chora-xp ends. A drag on the empty desktop draws XP's selection rectangle, in XP's selection blue with a translucent fill and a line of 1 pixel, and selects every icon whose picture or first line of its label it touches, while it grows and shrinks. A drag of one of the selected icons moves all of them, each to the cell at the same offset; if one of them would land on an icon that stays, or two in one cell, they all go back. A click on one of the selected icons selects it alone, and a click on the empty desktop selects nothing. Icons dropped on a window or on the Recycle Bin go back to their places: chora-xp changes no file. XP has one desktop, so the icons stay in place while the cube turns: each face of the cube shows them on the wallpaper.

The right button opens XP's context menus: white, with a gray border, a soft shadow and the selection in XP's blue. A click on a row does what it says and closes the menu; a click outside closes it. An open menu takes the keyboard. Up and Down move the highlight over the enabled rows. Right opens a submenu, Left closes it. Return does what the row says. Escape closes the submenu, then the menu. Home and End go to the first and the last row. Once a key works the menu, it underlines XP's access keys. A letter acts on the row of its access key, or goes to the next one of several. A drop-down list opens on its current value. While no window has the focus, the desktop takes the keyboard: Shift+F10 and the Menu key open the menu of the selected icon, or of the desktop.

  • The taskbar: Cascade Windows and Tile Windows Horizontally (one above the other) or Vertically (side by side) arrange the windows of the current desktop on the output of the menu; Show the Desktop minimizes them. Lock the Taskbar shows a check mark and changes nothing else, because chora-xp neither moves nor sizes the taskbar. Toolbars and Task Manager are gray: chora-xp has neither.
  • The clock: Adjust Date/Time, then the rows of the taskbar. Customize Notifications is gray.
  • The desktop: Arrange Icons By Name or Type puts the icons back into their columns, in that order; Refresh shows them again; Properties opens Display Properties (see below). Paste and Paste Shortcut are gray.
  • An icon of the desktop: the right button selects the icon and opens XP's menu of its kind. When the icon is part of the selection, the selection stays. The rows act on the icon under the pointer. Open, in bold, does what a double click does. The other rows are gray, among them Delete and Empty Recycle Bin: the file manager does that.
  • A program or a place of the start menu, or a program of All Programs: Open in bold, and Remove from This List for the programs of the left column except Terminal, which removes the program from the setting programs. Run as, Pin to Start menu, Send To and Rename are gray.

The Control Panel opens as a menu, as with XP's "Display as a menu". A check mark shows the current choice of each entry, and a click on an entry applies it and closes the menu. Desktop and Effects change the settings, as settings.set does:

  • Date and Time: opens Date and Time Properties;
  • Desktop: the wallpaper of every output, from the PNG, JPEG and SVG files in wallpapers/WindowsXP of the XDG data directories, theme/wallpaper/ and /usr/share/backgrounds, without their subdirectories and at most 20 of each directory;
  • Display: opens Display Properties;
  • Effects: wobbly windows, the magic lamp, the desktop cube and XP's sounds, on or off;
  • Taskbar and Start Menu: opens Taskbar and Start Menu Properties.

Properties of the taskbar menu, and Control Panel > Taskbar and Start Menu, open XP's Taskbar and Start Menu Properties. chora-xp draws this dialog itself, in XP's Luna style: the frame of the theme with the title and the close button, tabs, group boxes, check boxes, radio buttons and push buttons that light up under the pointer. A drag of the title bar moves it, and it wobbles as a window does, as do Date and Time, Display Properties and the other dialogs that XP lets move; the Log Off and Turn Off dialogs stay fixed in the middle. The close button and Cancel close it without a change, OK takes the changes and closes it, and Apply takes them and keeps it open. OK and Apply change the setting taskbar, as settings.set does. The dialog stays above the windows, and the keyboard does not work it (D45):

  • Taskbar shows a preview of the taskbar above its check boxes. Lock the taskbar only changes the check mark, as in the context menu. Auto-hide the taskbar lets the taskbars slide away half a second after the pointer left them, down to a strip of 2 pixels at the bottom edge; the pointer on the strip brings a taskbar back. The work area then reaches down to the strip, and maximized windows grow into it. Keep the taskbar on top of other windows puts the taskbars above the windows, or below them when it is off. Show the clock shows the clock in the notification area, or shrinks the area without it. Group similar taskbar buttons, Show Quick Launch, Hide inactive icons and Customize are gray: chora-xp has neither grouping, Quick Launch nor hidden icons.
  • Start Menu shows a preview of the start menu. The Classic Start menu and the Customize buttons are gray: chora-xp has only XP's start menu.

A double click on the clock, Adjust Date/Time of the clock menu and Control Panel > Date and Time open XP's Date and Time Properties, drawn in the same way:

  • Date & Time shows the month in a drop-down list and the year with arrow buttons, the month calendar with weeks from Sunday and the chosen day in blue, the analog clock with its moving hands and the digital time. A click on the list opens the twelve months, the arrows change the year and a click on a day chooses it. Below, it names the time zone of the system: TZ, else the link /etc/localtime.
  • Time Zone shows the zone with its offset from GMT. XP's world map is left out.

chora cannot set the clock of the system without privileges, so the dialog changes nothing: OK, Cancel and the close button close it, and Apply stays gray. Internet Time is left out.

Properties of the desktop menu and Control Panel > Display open XP's Display Properties, 404 by 455 pixels, drawn in the same way. It opens on the tab that was open when it last closed, Themes the first time. Apply and OK change the setting wallpaper, as settings.set does, and set the scale of the output of the dialog with output.configure of the core. Cancel and the close button close it without a change:

  • Themes shows the sample of the theme: the wallpaper with an active window and the Recycle Bin. Windows XP is the only theme, so the list, Save As and Delete are gray.
  • Desktop shows XP's monitor with the chosen background, and the list Background: (None) and the wallpapers of Control Panel > Desktop, with arrows and a track that scroll it. A click on a row chooses it. Position places the picture: Center at its own size in the middle, Tile repeated from the top-left corner, Stretch over the screen out of its aspect ratio, and Fill, which XP lacks, over the screen at its aspect ratio with the overflow cut off, as Windows 7 names it. Fill is the default, so that Bliss keeps its shape on a wide output; XP's own default is Stretch. Color chooses the color of the desktop behind a centered picture, or without one, from a palette of twelve colors with XP's desktop blue first. Browse is gray: chora-xp has no file chooser yet. Customize Desktop is gray too.
  • Screen Saver shows the monitor and XP's controls, all gray: chora-xp has no screen saver and no power settings.
  • Appearance shows a sample with an inactive window, an active window and a message box on the color of the desktop. The style, the color scheme and the font size are gray, as is Advanced. Effects opens a small dialog with check boxes for the wobbly windows, the magic lamp, the desktop cube and the sounds, as Control Panel > Effects; OK changes the setting effects.
  • Settings shows the monitor with the desktop and a taskbar, and the name of the output. The slider of Screen resolution chooses the scale of the output, 200 %, 150 %, 125 % or 100 % from Less to More, and names the size that it gives, such as "1280 by 800 pixels". Color quality, Troubleshoot and Advanced are gray.

Log Off and Turn Off Computer open XP's dialogs in the middle of the output, and the desktop behind them fades to gray in 1.5 seconds. They are modal: the start menu, the switcher and the system menu wait until they close, and the method start_menu fails meanwhile. As on XP, they have no default button and take no keys: Return does nothing, a click chooses. Each button runs its command of the setting session (D63):

Button Default command Without a command (null) Turn Off systemctl poweroff ends chora-xp and shuts nothing down Restart systemctl reboot runs chora-xp again, as the method restart does Stand By systemctl suspend disabled Log Off choractl quit, which ends chora through the core method session.quit asks every window to close and ends chora-xp

Stand By is also disabled when the first word of its command is not on the PATH. A command such as loginctl terminate-session $XDG_SESSION_ID ends a login session. Switch User is always disabled, because chora has no second session to switch to. Cancel or a click outside the dialog closes it. The buttons light up under the pointer; the keyboard does not work the dialogs (D45).

The method restart runs chora-xp again in the same process, with the same arguments, and so reads the settings file again. The core keeps the nodes of chora-xp for the grace time of resume (see API). The windows keep their places, desktops, maximized state and stacking, and the opacity and effects that other clients asked for. The current desktop stays, and its top window gets the focus.

Another client changes the opacity, the effects or the meta of an XP window with an update of the surface or of its group xp-win-ID (D58). chora-xp puts the opacity and the effects on the group, so the frame looks the same as the window, and the meta on the node that the client named, except the key xp. The meta of a surface does not stay over a restart.

chora-xp serves notifications (org.freedesktop.Notifications on the session bus), so that notify-send and programs show XP's balloon tips: a pale yellow balloon with a black border above the notification area of the first output, with a tail towards the tray, the icon of the notification, a bold title, the text wrapped at 300 pixels and a close button. While a balloon shows, the notification area grows for its icon, or XP's information icon, left of the clock, as on XP, and the tail points at it. One balloon shows at a time, and the others wait their turn. A balloon closes after its time, which is 10 seconds by default and, as on XP, at least 10 and at most 30 seconds; with a time of 0 it stays until a click. A click on the close button dismisses it; a click on the balloon invokes the action default of the notification, if it has one, and dismisses it too. If another server, such as GNOME Shell, owns the name on the bus, chora-xp logs one line and shows no balloons; it never takes the name from its owner.

The effects run in the plugin, which computes their meshes and transforms at 60 Hz:

  • Wobbly windows. A dragged window bends like jelly: the point under the pointer follows it, the far side lags behind, and after the release the window shakes until it settles.
  • Magic lamp. Minimize pours the window into its task button, and a click on the button pours it out again.
  • Desktop cube. Four desktops sit on the faces of a cube. A turn shows the cube in perspective, and the windows fly off their faces and land again. The taskbar lists the windows of the current desktop.

If frames get too slow because of chora-xp, the core drops its effects; chora-xp then goes without them for 15 seconds. A drop of the effects of another client changes nothing.

Binding Action Alt+F4 close the focused window Ctrl+Escape open or close the start menu Alt+Space open the system menu of the focused window; chora-xp takes the key only while one of its windows has the focus Alt+Tab, Alt+Shift+Tab open XP's switcher with the windows of the desktop, the most recent first. Tab chooses the next window, Shift+Tab the previous window. The release of Alt activates the chosen window. Minimized windows come last. Escape closes the switcher without a switch. Super+e start the terminal Ctrl+Alt+Left, Ctrl+Alt+Right turn the cube to the previous or next desktop Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Left, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Right turn the cube and take the focused window along Super and a drag with the left button turn the cube with the pointer. A drag over the width of the output is a quarter turn. At the release, the cube turns to the nearest desktop. a desktop button 1 to 4 turn the cube to that desktop

The safety layer keeps only Ctrl+Alt with BackSpace, Escape, i and F1 to F12, so the cube takes Ctrl+Alt with the arrows. Ctrl+Alt+i is the revoke binding of Safety layer. When another client holds these bindings, Super+Ctrl with the arrows stands in.

chora-xp exports methods for other clients (see Plugin methods). Each one answers with nothing.

Method Parameters Does the same as start_menu open: whether the menu should be open afterwards a click on the start button of the first output minimize surface a click on the task button of the active window restore, activate surface a click on the task button: the window comes back, is raised and focused, and the cube turns to its desktop restart none Restart in the Turn Off dialog without a command: chora-xp runs again and reads its settings file turn_to desktop: a number from 0 to 3 a click on the desktop button settings.get, settings.set, settings.reload see API the dialogs and an edit of the file with restart Option Default Meaning --theme DIR /usr/share/chora/flavors/xp/theme, or CHORA_XP_THEME the theme directory --config FILE chora/chora-xp.yaml in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME the settings file --slow-motion FACTOR 1 stretch the magic lamp and the cube, to show them slowly --output NAME all outputs manage only this output; repeat for more

chora-xp reads chora/chora-xp.yaml in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME, by default ~/.config, or the file of --config. Without a file, it uses its default, plugins/chora-xp/xp.yaml of the source tree. The file holds the settings of D62: settings.set and the dialogs change them at once and write the file again, without its comments. Edits by hand apply with the method settings.reload or restart. The default file lists every option; an option that the file leaves out takes its default:

Option Default Meaning terminal foot the terminal of Super+e and of Terminal at the top of the start menu; CMD -e runs the programs with Terminal=true launcher fuzzel Run in the start menu, and All Programs when no desktop file lists a program file_manager thunar the file manager of the places of the start menu and of the folder icons; chora-xp adds the folder to the command programs none the programs at the top left of the start menu below Terminal, each with title, command and icon, the name of an icon of the icon theme clock_format %-I:%M %p the clock of the taskbar, in the format of strftime, at most 64 characters wallpaper Bliss if installed, else Bløff picture: default, none or {file: PATH} with an absolute path of a PNG, JPEG or SVG file; position: center, tile, stretch or fill; color: red, green and blue of the desktop taskbar locked, on top, with the clock locked, auto_hide, on_top and clock, as Taskbar and Start Menu Properties effects all on wobbly, lamp, cube and sounds, as Control Panel > Effects session see above the commands of turn_off, restart, stand_by and log_off; null for none

settings.set merges its object into the settings (see API), so a change of the wallpaper names only what changes:

choractl call xp settings.set \
  '{"wallpaper": {"picture": {"file": "/usr/share/backgrounds/a.png"}}}'

To try the flavor from a source tree, start it nested:

cargo build --workspace
PATH=$PWD/target/debug:$PATH chora -- chora-xp --theme flavors/xp/theme

docs.title: Services
docs.text: A service runs as a Quadlet unit with Podman, or in distrobox. It connects to the IPC socket, appears as a Wayland client, or both. A container mounts only its client directory, which choractl clients create NAME makes (in Quadlet: %t/chora/clients/NAME). It sets CHORA_SOCKET to the ipc.sock and WAYLAND_DISPLAY to the wayland.sock in that directory. The directory of the core holds the admin socket, so a container never mounts it (see API). Through its ipc.sock, the container sees and changes only its own nodes and the windows of its wayland.sock. It sets no camera and puts no node under screen:*. It takes the keyboard with focus_node or focus only after a press of the user on it.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: The decision log. It lists the decisions that hold. Every entry can come back for review. The Roadmap names the milestone of a decision that the code does not implement yet.

docs.title: Principles and scope
docs.text: # Decision Reason D1 Rust and Smithay for the core Smithay is a library without policy, proven in niri and cosmic-comp. Rust is safe when agents change the system live. D2 Everything is a plugin Maximum flexibility and a small core. D3 chora 1.0 is a daily driver with a stable, versioned API; until then, the API changes without notice A stable API needs real use first. No compatibility code before 1.0. D4 Reuse before writing; check alternatives for every decision Little code to maintain. D5 One vocabulary, defined in the Glossary One language for people and agents. D6 Inventory and agent memory form a separate layer, not part of the core The platform stays neutral. D7 The name is chora, always in lowercase See Vision. D8 The core is GPL-3.0-or-later; code under GPL-3.0-only stays out The core can then reuse code from Pinnacle and niri. D9 English for code and documentation The documentation is public.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text: # Decision Reason D10 Fedora 44 and secureblue as host; a derived image offers chora as an additional session The system and the image tooling of the author. D11 The reference hardware is the HP ZBook Ultra G1a (AMD Radeon 8060S); CI adds a VM with vkms; Intel works through Mesa without a gate; NVIDIA comes later Gates need one machine that the author uses every day. The VM covers the tty backend in CI. D12 Services run as Quadlet units with Podman or in distrobox Isolation. systemd handles start, restart and order. D13 The coordinator is the user first, later an agent with special permissions A gradual path to control by agents. D14 Releases build an RPM and an Arch package, attached with SHA256 sums to a GitHub release; versions below 1.0 and release candidates are pre-releases One build for the release assets and the package repositories of D49.

docs.title: Core
docs.text: # Decision Reason D15 Build on Smithay; copy from Pinnacle, niri and anvil; no fork A fork of Pinnacle keeps less than half of its code. See Alternatives. D16 Pin a Smithay git revision No Smithay release since 0.7.0. All major users track git. D17 A scene renderer of chora on GLES 3, on the GL context of Smithay's GlesRenderer; GLSL shaders Smithay's render elements are axis-aligned rectangles. A renderer of its own draws the full 4x4 model and keeps textures between frames. wgpu has no usable dmabuf path for a compositor. D18 Six node kinds: group, surface, rect, image, shader and text Widgets come from Wayland clients. An image node shows a PNG asset, for example a window border, without a client per window. A shader can read another node as a texture. A text node lets plugins and agents label a HUD without a client or a rendered PNG. cosmic-text does the shaping and the font fallback, so the node stays small: text, font family, size, color and maximum width; no editing and no rich text. D19 Transforms are 4x4 matrices; the scene is 2.5D: planes in perspective, meshes and fragment shaders, without a depth test 3D effects need no API change. Complex 3D scenes belong in clients. D20 One logical scene; each output shows it through a camera Pan, zoom and the infinite canvas need no extra mechanism. D21 The core places popups, subsurfaces and layer surfaces; toplevels wait for a plugin The protocols define these positions. Smithay implements them. D22 A transaction completes when all affected clients commit, or after a deadline; transactions on disjoint surfaces do not wait for each other A resize needs a client round trip. One slow client must not stop the others. D23 A hardcoded safety layer: Ctrl+Alt+Backspace quits, Ctrl+Alt+Escape resets, Ctrl+Alt+F1 to F12 switch the VT, SIGUSR1 resets while the main loop runs; a watchdog that blames the client whose visible nodes cost the most for slow frames, removes its effects and then disconnects it, and never resets the session (D57); a watchdog thread on a heartbeat of the main loop for a hung loop (D64); a binding that revokes the capabilities of all clients A recovery path must not depend on a file that an agent can break, or on a main loop that hangs. One client without grants must not take the window manager, the grants and the effects of the others down with it. D24 The core renders an output only when it has damage; a layer keeps its texture until its subtree changes; a fullscreen surface without effects uses direct scanout Battery life and GPU load. D25 No undo history and no plugin state store in the core A destroyed client cannot come back. The reset and the views in git cover recovery. The scene holds all state. D26 Xwayland through xwayland-satellite Keeps the core small. D27 Output configuration through wlr-output-management and through output.configure, on the same path kanshi and wlr-randr exist. An agent has no wlr-randr in every session. D64 A watchdog thread watches a heartbeat that the main loop bumps after each dispatch; the loop wakes at least once a second. After 3 s without a beat, the thread logs the stall with the action that follows. After CHORA_HANG_ABORT_S seconds without a beat, 30 by default, it aborts chora with SIGABRT and a core dump, so that the session can start again; 0 means never abort. The stall and the abort lines go to fd 2 with a raw write(2), without the lock of tracing or of std::io::stderr. The SIGABRT handler then prints the backtrace of the watchdog thread, not that of the main loop; the core dump has all threads. The frame watchdog of D57 stays on the main loop A hung shader or driver blocks the main loop, so the frame watchdog and SIGUSR1 cannot act. Only another thread sees the hang. An abort ends the session, so the user can start it again, and leaves a core dump for the bug. 3 s is above the idle wake-up of 1 s and below the 5 s of the 0.9 gate. A main loop that hangs inside a log write holds the log lock, and the watchdog must not wait for it. A hang of 30 s is longer than any slow frame of llvmpipe, and the user waits no longer than that.

docs.title: Plugins and API
docs.text: # Decision Reason D28 Plugins are IPC clients; the core offers animate and frame events with the predicted presentation time; in-process WASM plugins come only after a measurement shows the need Agents work in seconds, not frames. One mechanism, any language, crash isolation by the OS. tests/ipc-bench.sh measures a transaction with a mesh of 8x8 cells at 0.17 ms in the median and 3.6 ms at the 99th percentile, nested and with software rendering. D29 JSON-RPC 2.0 with one message per line on Unix sockets; hello negotiates the protocol version and the features; errors carry a stable code and data Agents and shell scripts reach it without bindings. A versioned protocol lets plugins in other repositories check what they get. D30 The core starts one startup command with WAYLAND_DISPLAY and CHORA_SOCKET set The startup command starts the plugins, or a systemd target. D31 The owner of a node is a client name; only the owner changes a node; another client requests a change, and the core sends the request to the owner; plugins export methods with a description and a JSON schema An agent asks the window manager instead of fighting it. D32 Queries use JSON filters; a query returns all current matches; subscriptions start with a snapshot, and events have sequence numbers A schema describes the filters. Agents get predictable results and miss no event. D33 Each client has a socket directory with an IPC socket and a Wayland socket of its own that hides the privileged protocols; the socket fixes its name and its capabilities; input.inject, screen.capture, input.grab-any, methods.call, methods.privileged, activation.token and session.quit are capabilities A client cannot take another name or give itself capabilities. A container mounts one directory and needs no configuration. D34 MCP outside the core: choractl mcp over stdio on rmcp, with tools for whole tasks and one tool per exported plugin method The core stays free of MCP. The official SDK carries the protocol. D35 The core reads no configuration; choractl loads YAML views and ~/.config/chora/clients.yaml; a flavor is a directory with a systemd target; the configuration holds no secrets Policy and service management do not belong in the core. D36 The GitHub organization is chora-desktop (chora is taken). It holds chora (the core, chora-scene, choractl, the reference documentation), the plugins in repositories of their own, chora-website, chora-packaging, chora-voice and .github. The organization and this split come after 1.0; until the split, the core repository holds the core, the plugins and the services, and they build with it Plugins and services get their own owners and releases once the API of chora-scene is frozen at 1.0. The core keeps the definition of the API. D58 A client changes how a node of another client looks, its opacity, effects or meta, only through the owner: node.requested has the action update (D31). The window manager applies the change and keeps it across layouts. Clients on a confined client socket can send the request update, as move. An update that mixes owner-only props with opacity, effects or meta fails with an error that names the owner-only props. An update for an owner that does not subscribe to node.requested fails, because nobody would apply it. Requests for animate are not part of D58 The owner stays the only client that changes its nodes. A look that a new layout drops does not hold. D59 The answer of scene.apply carries warnings with stable codes, for example for a surface attached under a group with input: pass, or for a layer whose subtree (the layer and every layer under it) needs more pixels than the budget of every output; a drop at render time stays the event layers.dropped Some transactions succeed but do not give the result that the client expects. A warning tells the client without a capture. D61 choractl mcp keeps keep_nodes; after a restart, an agent removes its own old nodes (#101) No change in the core or in choractl. An agent knows which of its nodes still matter. D62 Each plugin exports settings.get and settings.set through the plugin runtime of chora-kit, with a schema in methods.export. The plugin checks the values, applies them at once and then saves them in its YAML file in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/chora/, for example chora-tiling.yaml and chora-xp.yaml; a change that cannot be applied is not saved, and a change that cannot be saved stays applied with an error to the caller. The plugin is the only writer of its file. A save renames a new file of mode 0600 over the old one; through a symlink, the save replaces the file that the symlink points to, so the symlink stays. Edits by hand apply with settings.reload, which the runtime exports with the other two methods and which reads the file again, or at the next start. settings.set takes a JSON merge patch (RFC 7386): structs and maps merge, other values replace, and null removes a map entry or resets a setting to its default. A setting that the file leaves out takes its default. The file replaces the command-line flags of chora-xp except --theme, --config, --slow-motion and --output. On a client socket, settings.set and settings.reload need the capability methods.privileged besides methods.call, because the settings hold commands that the plugin runs; so does each method that its export marks "privileged": true, such as app.open and scene.save of chora-mc, which start programs. A generic settings form is not part of 0.8 One interface serves choractl, MCP agents and the dialogs of the plugin. The file keeps the settings. D65 A client emits its own events with events.emit {event, data}. The name is the client name, a dot and a name of the client, for example voice.state; the core refuses any other name. A client whose name starts as a namespace of the core events, such as surface or output, emits nothing. The core sends the event with client and data to the connections that subscribed to its name or to a pattern PREFIX.*, such as voice.*. An empty subscription means every core event, not the events of clients. In events.subscribe, a name outside the core namespaces is the event of a client; a typo in a core name stays refused. The data has at most 64 KiB. A client name emits at most 32 events per second; the core refuses the rest with code 6 and does not coalesce, so a client sends the last state of a burst again. Any named client may emit, also through a client socket without capabilities, because an event only reaches subscribers. Any connection may subscribe to the events of other clients, by the same rules as core events, also a confined client socket. The voice agent emits voice.state (the agent.set fields; with name, a sub-agent such as coder) and voice.say (a sentence when its sound starts) on its connection voice; chora-mc subscribes to voice.* and keeps agent.set and hud.say for other clients A HUD needs the state of an agent when it changes, without polling and without a method of the HUD in the agent. The prefix makes the emitter visible: no client fakes a core event or the event of another name. A name of the main socket is still taken by whoever connects first; a client socket fixes it (D33). The limits protect the 8 MiB output buffer of a subscriber. A refusal tells the emitter; a silent drop would not.

docs.title: Tools around the core
docs.text: # Decision Reason D37 Screen sharing through xdg-desktop-portal-wlr No code. A portal backend of its own can come later. D38 HTML content from agents runs in a browser in app mode, as a service No code. chora places toplevels anywhere. D39 The XP showroom is a flavor in the style of Windows XP with wobbly windows, a magic lamp minimize and a 3D desktop cube; it lives in the core repository (D36); it is a demo on top of the generic plugins, not a daily driver; it starts installed programs, draws no programs into the scene except the dialogs of D63, and draws its own wallpaper, one per cube face; after its rework in 0.8, it gets fixes and the API ports of the core only, and no release per milestone It proves that the scene model carries classic desktops and their effects, and it tests every API change. The assets come from kde-plasma-winxp-launcher and keep their licenses; the GPL-3.0-only artwork of Exposé and modernXP is data of the flavor, not code of the core (D8). D40 The user gives capabilities in ~/.config/chora/clients.yaml; choractl clients up creates the client sockets through an admin socket that only choractl uses; the emergency reset removes all client sockets; choractl mcp has no tool for capabilities The core draws no text, so a dialog is no option. Only the user changes the capabilities. D41 choractl reads YAML with serde-saphyr: strict booleans, errors on unknown and duplicate keys and on unknown tags serde_yaml is archived and serde_yml is unsound. serde-saphyr is maintained, pure Rust and panic-free, and limits the work of a document. D42 The core starts no program except the startup command. choractl run starts programs through systemd-run --user with an activation token, and journald keeps their output. Without a running user manager, choractl run starts the program as its own child. systemd units restart plugins, and choractl restart restarts such a unit. systemd already supervises processes. Test sessions and sandboxes have no user manager; the fallback lives in choractl, so the core stays free of forks and one binary serves both. The activation token links a program to its window. D43 Nodes fixed to the screen live under one overlay root per output, screen:NAME: in the logical coordinates of the output, without its camera, above the scene and below the top and overlay layers of layer shell A HUD stays in place while a camera moves. A root per output answers on which output a node shows. Its nodes work as all others: input, effects, ownership. D44 output.configure sets scale and transform of an output through the API, on the same path as wlr-output-management One path keeps both ways in step. D45 Grabs need Ctrl, Alt or Super, except for a client with the capability input.grab-any; input.ungrab ends a grab; a key grab tells when the first of its modifiers goes up, except Shift; there is no exclusive keyboard grab Typing works unless the user gives a capability, for example for push-to-talk. Games and 3D clients get every key through Wayland. D63 chora-xp keeps the dialogs of the XP shell, pixel-perfect: Log Off, Turn Off, Display Properties, Taskbar and Start Menu Properties, Date and Time Properties and the Control Panel menu. Each button of Log Off and Turn Off runs a command from the settings (D62). The defaults are systemctl poweroff, systemctl reboot and systemctl suspend, and Log Off ends the chora session with choractl quit, which calls the core method session.quit. The dialogs change the settings through settings.set. The Explorer, the folder windows, file Properties and the Delete confirmation leave the plugin. My Documents, My Computer, folder icons and the Recycle Bin open the file manager of the settings, by default thunar. The tag archive/xp-scene-programs keeps the removed code. D63 refines D39 The dialogs are the showcase and the safeguard before a poweroff. A file manager drawn in the scene cannot match real file operations.

docs.title: Process
docs.text: # Decision Reason D46 Each milestone has a gate: CI jobs and checks on the reference hardware with a log as evidence, tracked in a gate issue; the next milestone of the core starts when the gate holds Breadth without real use hides faults. A gate makes "done" checkable. D47 The git flow of the project conventions: main holds chore: init and merge commits; work happens on dev, and each contributor of a shared repository has dev-NAME; a release is a merge into main and an annotated tag on the merge commit; the tag starts the release, which needs green CI of the same commit; commitizen writes the changelog; a review loop runs until a round finds nothing that matters; main accepts pull requests only from the move to the organization after 1.0 (D36) One flow in every repository. A release never ships a red commit. D48 The core is a library and a binary; IPC, transactions, focus and grants have unit tests with a fake clock; a headless GLES backend on the software driver of Mesa runs pixel tests in process; each bug fix comes with a test that fails without the fix Pixel tests in a headless sway cannot reach the internals. Review finds faults that tests should catch. D49 Packages through COPR with Packit, with a subpackage per plugin; no AUR packages The image build and updates need a package repository. D50 The session starts through uwsm; a flavor is a systemd target. While uwsm is not in Fedora 44, the sessions without uwsm (chora-session) are the fallback uwsm handles the environment and the graphical session target. D51 The daily driver of milestone 0.9 (D60) is chora-tiling with waybar, fuzzel, mako, swaybg, swaylock, swayidle and kanshi; panel and launcher plugins of chora come after 1.0 Existing tools cover the shell. Own plugins are no condition for 0.9 or 1.0. D52 The milestones run 0.6 to 1.0 as in the Roadmap A stable API needs real use and a testable core first. D53 The voice pipeline lives in chora-voice, until the split after 1.0 in services/voice/ of the core repository (D36), and runs in parallel to the core; the core supplies push-to-talk grabs, text injection, the read model and an agent indicator The pipeline is a product of its own. It needs only the API of the core. D54 Plugins use the JSON-RPC API with frame events and fd passing; a private Wayland protocol for plugins comes only if a measurement at 120 Hz in milestone 0.10 shows the need One API to maintain. The measurement decides. D55 Window managers share the scene through claims. A claim is a scene area of one window manager. A window manager hands a surface to another with remove and to. The core gives a new toplevel to a window manager (see below). The user chose one window manager per claim over a single window manager role. Ownership, attach and surface.detached stay the mechanism, and a camera switches between claims. D56 The UI is hybrid. Plugins draw shell chrome and effects as scene nodes. Real applications, such as a file manager or a control panel, run as Wayland clients. Scene nodes take the keyboard through focus_node. In 0.8, chora-xp stops drawing programs into the scene, except its dialogs, and starts installed programs instead (D39, D63). The git tag archive/xp-scene-programs keeps the removed code Chrome and effects need the scene: transforms, shaders, wobble. Applications need text input, accessibility and toolkits, which clients bring. D57 The watchdog disconnects a client for slow frames only when its own visible load reaches the owner budget, CHORA_OWNER_LOAD_BUDGET with a default of 4000. Below it the slowdown is shared: the watchdog removes the effects of all clients and disconnects none The W5 battle disconnected a playing snake while a budget probe churned its nodes. The largest single load was not the fault. Two clients that are each half the fault should keep their connections, and the frame still gets cheap; a client alone over its budget is the clear culprit. D60 The daily driver comes before the renderer: milestone 0.9 is the daily driver and 0.10 the renderer Daily use needs a stable session more than a faster renderer. 0.9 takes from the renderer only the watchdog thread, which detects a hung main loop.

docs.title: D55: window managers per claim
