docs.text: Issue #73 calls the area of a window manager a view. The glossary uses "view" for a YAML arrangement (D5), so this design says claim. The design has two steps. Step 1 is the handover. Step 2 adds claims and the routing of new toplevels.

docs.title: Step 1: handover
docs.text:
Window manager A hands surface s1 to window manager B:

  1. A owns s1, for example at the end of a drag out of its area. A knows B by a fixed name or by a meta tag on the root group of B.
  2. A sends remove: {id: s1, to: B}. to must name a connected client. As at every remove, the surface becomes detached and loses the keyboard focus.
  3. The core reserves s1 for B and sends surface.detached, which carries the surface alone. An attach of another client fails.
  4. B attaches s1, places it by its own rules, and can give it the focus. A plugin that adopts every detached surface needs no change.
  5. When the last connection of B closes, the reservation ends. With resume, it ends after the grace time. The core then sends surface.detached to all, and any client can attach the surface.

Focus and grabs. The keyboard focus does not move with the surface. The receiving window manager sets it with focus after the attach. Grabs belong to connections and do not move. A ends its drag at the release of the button, and then hands the surface over. The client of the surface keeps its pointer and keyboard input as before.

docs.title: Step 2: claims
docs.text:
A claim is a rectangle in scene coordinates: the property claim: [x, y, w, h] of a node. The owner of the node holds the claim. A window manager sets it on its root group, and the claim ends with its node. Window managers claim the whole work area of their outputs. An output shows a claim through its camera. So two window managers sit on two outputs, or at two places in the scene, and a camera move switches one output between them. With claims, A finds B in the claims of scene.query.

At the first commit of a toplevel, the core picks its window manager. The first choice is the owner of its parent toplevel, so that a dialog stays with the manager of its window. The next choice is the owner of the focused node, or of the focused surface, if it holds a claim. The last choice is the owner of the smallest claim that contains the pointer. A client that asked for an activation token (D42) does not win by the token itself. The core reserves the surface for that client, as at a handover. Outside of all claims, any window manager can take the new surface.

Out of scope for now.

  • The drop position: B places the surface by its own rules.
  • A drag that continues in B after the handover.
  • An embedded GNOME session in a claim.
  • Claims under screen:NAME.

A 3D node with depth buffer in the core It makes the core an engine. 3D scenes belong in clients (D19). A rewrite from scratch The scene model, the API and the safety layer hold. docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The shared vocabulary of chora. Code, docs and prompts to agents use these terms and no synonyms.

Term Meaning Core The compositor process chora. It handles the Wayland protocols, the backends (DRM/KMS, libinput), the scene, the renderer, the input routing, the IPC socket and the safety layer. It contains no policy. Scene The tree of nodes that the core renders. It is the single source of truth for the screen content. Node One element of the scene. The kinds are group, surface, rect, image, shader and text. Every node has an id, an owner, a transform, an opacity and optional effects. Group A node that contains other nodes. It applies a transform, a clip, an opacity and optional effects to its children. Canvas A group that serves as a working area: a workspace, a desktop or an infinite zoomable plane. Surface A node that shows a Wayland client: an application window, a layer-shell widget or a browser window. For the core, a surface is a texture source and an input target. Rect A colored rectangle with optional rounded corners and border. Shader A node that a fragment shader draws completely. A shader can read other nodes as textures. A shader can also be an effect. Effect A shader that changes how a node and its children look, for example blur or a color change. Every node can have effects. Camera The part of the scene that one output shows: a transform from scene coordinates to the logical coordinates of the output. Claim A scene area of one window manager (D55). Work area The part of the scene that an output shows, without the zones that panels and IPC clients reserve. Plugins place windows in it. Client A process on the IPC socket: a plugin, choractl or a service. A client names itself when it connects. Owner The client name that created or attached a node. Only the owner changes the node. Toplevel A surface with the role of an application window (xdg_toplevel). Other roles are layer surfaces and popups. Detached The state of a surface node without a parent. A detached surface is not visible. View A declarative arrangement: nodes, the plugins that drive them, and their configuration. A view is a YAML file in git. The user or an agent changes it live. Plugin A client that reacts to events, changes the scene and can export methods. A window manager, a layout, an animation set and a keybinding set are plugins. Service A process in a container, outside the core. Examples are speech recognition, a local LLM and a development environment. Flavor A preconfigured bundle of views, plugins and services, for example "classic", "tiling" or "agentic". Coordinator The party that installs and connects plugins, services and flavors. First the user, later an agent with special permissions. Inventory A local, git-versioned store of reusable elements (views, plugins, widgets). It belongs to the opinionated layer above chora, not to the core. Command A request to change the scene, for example create or update. Event A message from the core about a change, for example surface.created. Selector An expression that finds nodes by id, attribute or meta data, for example app_id:firefox. Transaction A batch of commands that the core applies as one unit. If one command fails, the core applies none of them. Capability A right of a client beyond the scene API: input.inject, screen.capture, input.grab-any, methods.call and activation.token. A client socket fixes the capabilities of its name (D33). Grant A capability that a client name holds: from choractl grant on the main socket, or from clients.yaml for a client socket. Milestone A minor release on the way to 1.0, with a goal, a scope and a gate. See Roadmap. Gate The checks that end a milestone; see Roadmap. Safety layer The only built-in behavior of the core: fixed bindings, emergency reset, session lock, watchdog.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
The layout of this repository: one Cargo workspace with as few crates as possible. A module moves into its own crate only when a second consumer can use it. The plugins move into repositories of their own with 1.0 (D36).

chora/
├── crates/
│   ├── chora-scene/   # scene model, commands, events, selectors, IPC types and client; no Smithay
│   ├── chora/         # the compositor: Smithay, backends, renderer, input, safety, IPC
│   ├── chora-kit/     # building blocks for plugins: the plugin runtime, wobbly windows, magic lamp, XDG dirs, icons, desktop entries
│   └── choractl/      # CLI over the IPC socket; `choractl mcp` is the MCP bridge
├── plugins/
│   ├── chora-tiling/  # reference plugin: the tags, layouts and bindings of awesome
│   ├── chora-xp/      # stacking window manager in the style of Windows XP
│   └── chora-mc/      # experimental: a voice-first desktop, one full-screen scene at a time
├── flavors/           # systemd units of the flavors; the theme of the XP flavor
├── examples/          # loader prototype and showcase apps over the API
├── services/voice/    # the voice agent and the quadlets of its models
├── dist/              # RPM build script, Fedora build requirements, session files, Quadlet examples
├── tests/             # end-to-end scripts, headless sessions, input probe
├── deny.toml          # cargo-deny: allowed licenses, advisories
├── ruff.toml          # ruff: the rules for the Python in services/voice/
├── docs/              # this documentation (MkDocs)
├── mkdocs.yml
└── Cargo.toml         # workspace, lints

docs.title: Reasons for this split
docs.text:
• chora-scene has no Smithay dependency. Tests of the data model and the transaction logic need no GPU and no compositor. The core, choractl and plugins share this one definition of the API.
  • chora-kit holds the building blocks that plugins share and that are not part of the API of the core: the IPC and event connection, the plugin runtime, the self-computed effects and the freedesktop files. Code of one plugin stays in that plugin.
  • Reference plugins are workspace members. They keep the API honest.
  • choractl builds the JSON schemas from the Rust types at run time, in crates/choractl/src/schema.rs. The repository does not contain them. The MCP tools and the test of the documentation examples then see the same contract.

docs.text: The path from the current state to chora 1.0. Version 1.0 is a daily driver with a stable, versioned API (D3).

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Each milestone is a minor release: 0.6, 0.7 and so on.
  • Each milestone has a goal, a scope, an estimate and a gate.
  • A milestone gets a firm estimate when its scope is fixed. The table holds a first guess.
  • The gate is a list of checks. A check is a CI job or a step on the reference hardware with a log as evidence (D46).
  • A milestone is done when every check of its gate holds. The next milestone of the core starts only then.
  • Each milestone has a gate issue on GitHub with the checks as a task list. Each ticked check links to its CI run or log. The release of the milestone closes the issue.
  • Two tracks run in parallel to the core: the XP showroom and the voice pipeline.
  • The showroom track has no milestones of its own (see Track: XP showroom).
  • The voice track has milestones of its own. It never blocks the core.

docs.title: Current state
docs.text:
• The core runs nested and as a login session. It has no long run on real hardware.
  • The scene has six node kinds, 4x4 transforms, cameras, overlay roots, meshes, effects and animations.
  • The API covers scene changes, events, grabs, plugin methods, captures, input injection, grants, programs, assets and output configuration.
  • choractl loads views and serves MCP.
  • chora-tiling and the XP showroom are plugins in this repository.
  • The core is a library and a binary. Unit tests run IPC dispatch, transactions, focus and grants in process, without a backend. The tty backend has no tests. One pixel test renders in process on the headless backend. Pixel tests in a headless sway check the behavior.

docs.title: Estimates
docs.text:
The estimates count the lines of Rust that a milestone adds or changes. They also count the hours of agent work and the hours of hands-on work of the user. The calendar time includes the gate. Agent hours include the tests and the review rounds.

The basis is this repository: about 26,000 lines of Rust in 54 hours of calendar time. A rework of existing code costs more than new code. The table uses about 140 to 200 lines per agent hour for 0.6, 0.7 and 0.10. The milestones 0.9 and 1.0 have hardware work and use about 80 to 125.

The user uses chora as the daily session from milestone 0.9. The gates of 0.9 and 1.0 measure that use, so they set the calendar time.

docs.title: 0.6: Foundation
docs.text:
Released as v0.6.0 on 2026-10-19 without the gate checks 1, 2 and 5. These checks moved to the gate of 0.7. Check 1 then moved to the time after 1.0, with the organization (D36).

The organization and the protected main moved to after 1.0 (D36, D47).

Goal: the project works with gates in the GitHub organization chora-desktop. Unit tests check the core in process.

Scope:

  • The organization chora-desktop with the core repository (D36). The split of the plugins into repositories of their own is postponed past 0.6; the plugins build with the core.
  • camera.release on the admin socket: the administrator takes the camera of an output from its owner, live or gone.
  • One socket directory per client: $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/chora/clients/NAME/ with ipc.sock and a Wayland socket wayland.sock (D33, D40). The socket fixes the name of its clients. choractl clients up applies a clients.yaml. The emergency reset removes the client sockets. An example Quadlet unit in dist/ shows an agent container that mounts its client directory.
  • The ipc.sock of a client socket narrows the scene: its connections see and change only their own nodes and windows. They set no camera, use no screen:* parent, and use focus_node only after a press.
  • The capability input.grab-any allows grabs without Ctrl, Alt or Super (D45).
  • surface.created carries the pid and the activation token.
  • An unknown event name in events.subscribe is an error.
  • The git flow of D47 in every repository: a protected main, releases from a merge commit and an annotated tag.
  • The release workflow starts from a tag and needs a green CI run of the same commit.
  • A pinned Rust toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml, a job for the minimum Rust version, and container images pinned by digest.
  • The core as a library and a binary (D48). IPC dispatch, the transaction queue, focus and grants run in unit tests with a fake clock.
  • A headless test backend that renders with GLES on the software driver of Mesa in process, for pixel tests in Rust. GLES checks the same render path as the screen.
  • A smoke test in a VM with vkms in CI (D11). chora starts on the tty backend and shows a foot window. A capture shows its pixels.
  • The reference documentation stays with the code of the core; the website repository follows with the split (D36).

Gate:

  1. The organization chora-desktop and the core repository exist, and main accepts pull requests only.
  2. A test release v0.6.0-rc.1 comes from a tag on a merge commit. A tag on a commit with red CI starts no release.
  3. cargo test runs at least 40 unit tests of the core crate for IPC, transactions, focus and grants, without a compositor.
  4. One pixel test runs in process on the headless backend.
  5. The vkms job is green in 10 runs in a row.
  6. tests/nested.sh, tests/agent.sh and tests/xp.sh are green in CI.
  7. rust-toolchain.toml pins the toolchain, and the job for the minimum Rust version is green.
  8. Every container image in the workflows has a digest.

docs.title: 0.7: Identity, processes and the basics of the read model
docs.text:
The release candidate v0.7.0-rc.3 is tagged. No check of the 0.7 gate is open.

Goal: a client cannot take another name or give itself capabilities, the core starts no programs, and an agent can see focus and geometry without guessing. An agent can ask the window manager for changes, and it can label what it shows.

Scope:

  • The client socket also fixes the capabilities of its clients: the socket decides which methods a connection may use (D33).
  • A versioned hello with the protocol version and the features of both sides (D29). Until then hello answers with the version of the build, and the client library warns on a mismatch.
  • Stable error codes: one code for each kind of failure. The error data already names the failed command.
  • The core starts no program except its startup command (D42).
  • Focus in queries: the surface and the node that have the keyboard.
  • Queries return the screen rectangle of a node on each output.
  • choractl wait SELECTOR returns when a node matches, or fails after a timeout.
  • input.inject keeps a button down across requests with hold, so that a drag can span several requests. A dry run checks a batch without applying it.
  • chora-tiling exports methods for tags, focus and moves. chora-xp exports methods for the start menu, minimize, restore and Restart.
  • JSON filters next to the selector strings (D32). They can match focus and visibility.
  • events.subscribe starts with a snapshot of the state, and every event has a sequence number seq.
  • input.inject takes a node and a point inside it.
  • A client that does not own a node can request a change: focus, move, resize or close. The core sends the request to the owner as the event node.requested, and the owner decides (D31). chora-tiling handles the requests.
  • Plugin methods carry a description and a JSON schema. choractl mcp makes one tool from each method (D34).
  • choractl mcp uses rmcp, answers requests in parallel and supports cancellation.
  • Text injection commits a text into the text input of the focused surface, also characters that the current keymap does not have.
  • A visible indicator while a client injects input, and a binding of the safety layer that revokes the capabilities of all clients (D23).
  • The text node on cosmic-text (D18).
  • Small fixes from the battle test: compact JSON from choractl run, a clear error from clients create for a taken name, chora-probe --exit-on-close, and tests/ipc-bench.sh on the headless session.

Gate:

  1. Moved to the time after 1.0: the organization and the protected main (D36).
  2. A test release v0.7.0-rc.1 comes from a tag on a merge commit. A tag on a commit with red CI starts no release (from 0.6).
  3. The vkms job is green in 10 runs in a row (from 0.6).
  4. A Podman container that mounts only clients/agent/ queries the scene and draws a node. Its grants.set and its hello with another name fail. A CI job checks this.
  5. Moved to the gate of 0.8: the Quadlet unit after a restart of chora.
  6. A client with input.grab-any grabs F13 and a letter key. A client without it gets the error code for a missing capability.
  7. The core has no code that forks a process except the startup command.
  8. Without a user manager, choractl run foot starts foot directly, and the surface.created event of its window carries the activation token. The case with a user manager moved to the gate of 0.8.
  9. Each error code of the API has a test that provokes it.
  10. The battle workflows in tests/battle/ pass with choractl wait, the focus and the rectangles of queries and the plugin methods, without pixel clicks.

The scripts tests/gate-0.8-N.sh below are checks of the 0.7 gate. They check the delivered scope. The scripts keep their own numbers, which differ from the numbered 0.7 checks:

  • tests/gate-0.8-1.sh: An MCP client in CI calls the tools to focus the second terminal and to request a move to the right. chora-tiling performs both, and a capture shows them.
  • tests/gate-0.8-2.sh: Under a camera with pan and zoom, a click on a node through the MCP tools hits that node in 20 of 20 tries.
  • tests/gate-0.8-3.sh: wait_events returns while another tool call runs, and a cancelled call ends within 100 ms.
  • tests/gate-0.8-4.sh: Injected text Grüße äöüß appears unchanged in foot on a US layout. A CI job checks this.
  • tests/gate-0.8-5.sh: A subscription that starts during a transaction misses no event and sees no event twice: a test with 1,000 transactions checks the sequence numbers.
  • tests/gate-0.8-6.sh: The tool list of choractl mcp matches the exported methods of the plugins after each methods.export.
  • tests/gate-0.8-7.sh: A capture shows the indicator while a client injects input.
  • tests/gate-0.8-8.sh: A test shows that the revoke binding removes the capabilities of all clients.
  • tests/gate-0.8-9.sh: A text node shows Grüße 你好 🙂 with fallback fonts, and a pixel test against a reference capture passes.
  • tests/gate-0.8-10.sh: An MCP client puts a text node under screen:NAME, and a capture shows it.

docs.title: 0.8: Lean plugins and the agent API
docs.text:
Goal: lean plugins on a shared runtime, and the agent API gaps.

Scope:

  • chora-xp draws no programs into the scene (D63). The Explorer, the folder windows, file Properties and the Delete confirmation leave the plugin. The git tag archive/xp-scene-programs keeps this code.
  • chora-xp keeps the dialogs of the XP shell, pixel-perfect (D63): Log Off, Turn Off, Display Properties, Taskbar and Start Menu Properties, Date and Time Properties and the Control Panel menu. The buttons of Log Off and Turn Off run the commands of the settings.
  • A shared plugin runtime in chora-kit: the reconnect loop, the startup with output.list, events.subscribe and methods.export, grabs, the export and dispatch of methods, and the --output filter. Claims and the resume from meta go into the runtime only where both plugins use them in the same way.
  • The settings interface of D62 for both plugins: settings.get and settings.set through the runtime, with a schema in methods.export, and the YAML file of the plugin.
  • chora-tiling is the lean reference window manager on the runtime. Its default style for new windows is a setting (#99).
  • chora-xp moves onto the runtime and the settings. The settings file replaces most of its command-line flags; Configuration lists the others. Its dialogs change the settings with settings.set.
  • The start menu and double clicks of chora-xp start installed programs. My Documents, My Computer, folder icons and the Recycle Bin open the file manager of the settings, by default Thunar.
  • chora-xp keeps the XP look: frames, taskbar, start menu, the XP notification balloons, wallpaper, sounds and the cube (D39).
  • The action update of node.requested changes opacity, effects and meta of a node through its owner (D58). The window manager keeps the change across layouts (#97).
  • The answer of scene.apply carries warnings (D59): a surface attached under a group with input: pass (#98), and a layer whose subtree needs more pixels than the budget of every output (#100).
  • docs/api.md tells agents to remove their own old nodes after a restart (D61).
  • Bugs of choractl mcp: #53, #54 and #56.
  • The hardware checks 5 and 8 of the 0.7 gate.

The work removes the XP programs first, then extracts the runtime and the settings from chora-tiling, and then ports chora-xp to both.

Gate:

  1. No plugin crate (chora-tiling, chora-xp) has a reconnect loop or calls methods.export, output.list or events.subscribe. CI checks this with a grep over plugins/. The battle workflows in tests/battle/ and tests/xp.sh pass.
  2. The program modules of chora-xp are gone: explorer.rs, explorer/view.rs, folder.rs, wm/explorers.rs, properties.rs and confirm.rs. The tag archive/xp-scene-programs exists.
  3. The start menu of chora-xp starts the file manager of its settings, and the surface.created event of its window carries the activation token. The check runs in CI in the e2e container, without a user manager. The container installs Thunar from Fedora 44 as the file manager.
  4. choractl sets a setting of chora-xp, for example the wallpaper, with settings.set (D62). A capture shows the change at once. After a restart of the plugin, the YAML file holds the value. A wrong value gets an error. A CI job checks this.
  5. A client sets the opacity of a tiling window to 0.5 with the action update of node.requested (D58). After a relayout, a query or a capture in CI shows the opacity 0.5.
  6. settings.set changes the default style of chora-tiling, and a new window gets this style (#99). A CI job checks this.
  7. scene.apply answers with a warning code for a surface attached under a group with input: pass (D59). It also answers with a warning code for a layer whose subtree (the layer and every layer under it) needs more pixels than the budget of every output (#100). Unit tests check both.
  9. A Quadlet unit from dist/ connects through its client directory after a restart of chora, without a change to the unit. The user runs this check on the reference hardware, with a log.
  10. With a user manager, choractl run foot starts foot in a transient systemd unit of its own, and the surface.created event of its window carries the activation token. The user runs this check on the reference hardware, with a log.
  11. CI runs the CI scripts of the earlier gates again. The user runs the hardware checks again on the reference hardware, with a log.

docs.title: 0.9: Daily driver
docs.text:
Goal: the user works in chora every day on the reference hardware (D60).

Scope:

  • The session starts through uwsm (D50). A flavor is a systemd target. uwsm is not in Fedora 44, so the sessions without uwsm (chora-session) are the fallback.
  • The tiling flavor: chora-tiling with waybar, fuzzel, mako, swaybg, swaylock, swayidle and kanshi (D51).
  • Input device settings through the API: tap, acceleration, natural scroll, key repeat. A view sets them, so the core reads no file (D35).
  • Output hotplug, suspend and resume, lid switch, and the VT switch on the reference hardware.
  • Screen sharing through xdg-desktop-portal-wlr, and X11 apps through xwayland-satellite.
  • The install from the release RPM, layered on secureblue (D10, D14).
  • The stability bugs #14, #31, #32, #50, #57 and #60.
  • From the renderer: the watchdog in its own thread with a heartbeat of the main loop (D23, #89).

Gate:

  1. The user works 10 working days in a row only in chora on the reference hardware. coredumpctl list chora shows no entry, and the log shows no emergency reset that the user did not start.
  2. A shader node with an endless loop runs on llvmpipe in CI. The watchdog thread logs the stall within 6 s. The log line names the action, and a test checks it.
  3. A main loop that blocks for 5 s triggers the watchdog. A test with a debug hook checks it.
  4. A checklist on the reference hardware passes, with the log of each step. An external monitor goes in and out 10 times, and the laptop suspends and resumes 10 times. The user closes and opens the lid, switches the VT, and locks and unlocks the session. A screen share in a browser and an X11 app work.
  5. The vkms job covers hotplug of a second output.
  6. A view sets tap and key repeat, and a test shows that the core applies them.
  7. CI runs the CI scripts of the earlier gates again. The user runs the hardware checks again on the reference hardware, with a log, except the daily-use checks (0.9 gate 1).
  8. chora installs from the release RPM, layered on secureblue with rpm-ostree, and starts as a uwsm session with the tiling flavor. The log of the reference hardware shows both steps.

docs.title: 0.10: Renderer
docs.text:
Goal: the core renders only what changed, draws the full 4x4 model, and drives plugins with the frame clock (D17, D24).

Scope:

  • A retained scene: each node keeps its world transform, its bounds and its render resources. Integer handles replace string keys inside the renderer.
  • A scene renderer of chora on GLES 3. It draws each node as a quad with its full matrix. Rounded corners, borders and clips come from signed distance fields in the same pass.
  • A layer renders offscreen only for group opacity, effects or an explicit cache. A layer keeps its texture until its subtree changes. Textures have mipmaps, and their resolution follows the size on screen.
  • A redraw state machine per output. Without damage, the output renders nothing and the loop sleeps. A fullscreen surface without effects goes to direct scanout.
  • Frame events with the predicted presentation time for subscribed plugins (D28). Animations run on the same clock. They interpolate translation, rotation and scale apart, run per property, and support springs.
  • Transactions on disjoint surfaces do not wait for each other (D22).
  • A render thread (#35).
  • Shader compile and capture encode run on worker threads, as the image decode does.
  • Debug counters for rendered frames and texture allocations, readable through the API.
  • fd passing for images and captures over the IPC socket (D54).
  • A measurement of the plugin round trip at 120 Hz decides on a private Wayland protocol for plugins (D54).
  • The bugs of the render quality: #34, #36, #37, #38, #46, #47, #48, #74, #75, #76, #78 and #79.

Gate:

  1. A static scene with rounded windows, a clipped group and a blurred panel renders 0 frames in 10 s of idle time. A counter of the core shows it, in CI and on the reference hardware.
  2. On the reference hardware at the refresh rate of the internal panel: four windows with blur and rounded corners and a 300 ms transition. presentation-time shows 99 percent of the frames on time over 60 s.
  3. A node with rotation and no size renders. A camera with zoom 2 keeps text sharp: a pixel test against a reference capture passes.
  4. A size animation of a layer over 2 s allocates no new texture after the first frame. A counter of the texture pool shows it.
  5. A client that delays its commit for 150 ms delays no transaction of another client. A unit test checks it.
  6. A test client runs the wobbly window and magic lamp code of chora-kit on frame events. At 60 Hz and at 120 Hz in CI, 99 percent of its frames are on time over 30 s.
  7. The decision on the plugin protocol is in the decision log, with the measurement.
  8. CI runs the CI scripts of the earlier gates again. The user runs the hardware checks again on the reference hardware, with a log, except the daily-use checks (0.9 gate 1).

docs.title: 1.0: Stable API
docs.text:
Goal: the API is version 1 and stays compatible until 2.0.

Scope:

  • The protocol version 1: a JSON schema of all methods, events and errors in the repository, generated from chora-scene. A CI job fails on a change of the schema without a change of the protocol version.
  • The reference documentation comes from the schema. A test checks every example of the documentation against it.
  • A client socket (D33) moves the keyboard focus only after a press of the user. The window manager that owns a surface, and requests through node.requested, stay exempt (#102).
  • A failed grab names the client that holds the binding (#63).
  • Packages through COPR with Packit and subpackages per plugin (D49). The release keeps its assets.
  • The image of secureblue-images installs chora from COPR.
  • A final review loop over the whole code base until a round finds nothing that matters (D47).
  • All plugins of the core repository use the protocol version 1.

Gate:

  1. The user works 30 days with the release candidate as the daily session. coredumpctl list chora shows no entry.
  2. No open issue has the label severity:high.
  3. The last review round leaves no open finding of high or medium severity.
  4. The schema job and the documentation test are green.
  5. Every plugin of the core repository uses protocol version 1, and a CI job checks it.
  6. The secureblue image builds with chora from COPR. rpm-ostree upgrade on the reference hardware updates chora, and the login screen offers the session.
  7. CI runs the CI scripts of the earlier gates again. The user runs the hardware checks again on the reference hardware, with a log, except the daily-use checks (0.9 gate 1, 1.0 gate 1).

docs.title: Track: XP showroom
docs.text:
The showroom lives in the core repository (D39) and moves to chora-desktop/chora-xp with the split after 1.0 (D36). It shows the effects of the scene and serves as their test.

  • The showroom has no release per milestone. tests/xp.sh runs in the CI of the core.
  • After its rework in 0.8, the showroom gets fixes and the API ports of the core only (D39).

docs.title: Track: voice pipeline
docs.text:
The voice pipeline lives in services/voice/ of the core repository and moves to chora-desktop/chora-voice with the split after 1.0. It started with milestone 0.6 (D53). The models run as Quadlet units on the reference hardware: speech to text, a language model and text to speech, served by Gufo.

Milestone Goal Gate Needs from the core V1 Pipeline speech in, an answer as speech out, with barge-in median 1.0 s or less from the end of speech to the first audio, over 20 German utterances nothing V2 Control the voice agent drives chora through MCP "move the terminal to the right" works in 18 of 20 tries 0.7 (read model, text injection) V3 Views a morning view and task views "show my tasks for today" opens a view with the tasks of an MCP source; "open a view for the first task" opens a view with two surfaces 0.7

docs.title: After 1.0
docs.text:
• The organization chora-desktop (D36). The core repository moves there, and main accepts pull requests only (D47). The plugins, the XP showroom and the voice pipeline move into repositories of their own.
  • Small plugins that window managers share: a panel with a task list and the notifications, and a launcher (D51). Until then, shared code lives in chora-kit.
  • Conformance tests with wlcs.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: Three scenarios test the concept and estimate the effort on top of the core. The estimates are rough. They assume that the core implements the common Wayland protocols (see Dependencies), so existing tools work unchanged.

docs.title: 1. Classic desktop
docs.text:
A Windows-like desktop with taskbar, start menu and overlapping windows, driven by mouse and keyboard. This is not the goal of chora, but it must be possible.

Part Source Effort Stacking window manager: move, resize, raise, focus, minimize plugin about 1000 to 2000 lines Window decorations: title bar, buttons plugin with rect and shader nodes, a decoration surface of the plugin, or client-side decorations small to medium Keybindings: Alt+Tab, Super key plugin small Taskbar, tray, clock existing shell: Quickshell, waybar, eww configuration Start menu, launcher fuzzel, wofi or a Quickshell widget configuration Wallpaper swaybg or swww configuration Pixel-perfect XP look theme assets, shaders, decorations much detail work, little difficulty

The taskbar needs the foreign-toplevel protocols to see the windows. The launcher and the bar need wlr-layer-shell.

Result: medium effort, almost all of it in one window manager plugin.

docs.title: 2. Keyboard-driven tiling
docs.text:
A Linux-style tiling workflow with workspaces. The user configures it.

Part Source Effort Tiling layout: master and stack, columns, scrolling plugin a few hundred lines Workspaces one group per workspace, switched by visibility or transform small Keybindings, focus movement plugin small Bar waybar or Quickshell configuration Animations the animate command of the core small

Result: low effort. This is a good first flavor to test the plugin API.

docs.title: 3. Agentic workday
docs.text:
This scenario is the core idea. A robust voice channel connects the user to an agent, and the agent arranges content for each task.

  1. Morning view. The agent greets the user and shows the current tasks. It sorts the email. User and agent plan and prioritize the day together.
  2. Task views. The agent builds a new canvas for each task and fills it. A data analysis gets prepared data, plots and interactive exploration. Email, web research and coding get their own views.
  3. Reuse. The inventory keeps useful elements in git for later use. The agent discards code for one-time use.
  4. Live change by voice. "Make the plot bigger." "Put the terminal next to the notebook." "Dim everything except the editor." The agent calls the methods of the window manager plugin for these changes.
Part Source Effort Scene access for the agent IPC socket and choractl mcp part of the API Speech in and out the voice pipeline of chora-voice (D53) integration The agent Claude Code or another MCP client, later a local LLM service integration Rich content: greeting, plots, email the agent writes HTML, a browser in app mode shows it as a surface generated content Data exploration Jupyter, marimo or a plot web app as surfaces existing tools One view per task YAML views that choractl loads, saves and changes live coordinator tool Inventory, memory opinionated layer above chora later

Result: the largest scenario, but mostly integration of existing parts. The core must supply scene queries and changes, screenshots and input injection. The agent needs screenshots to see the result of its changes.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
• The six node kinds cover all three scenarios.
  • Widgets and rich content do not need to live in the core. Existing shells, wallpaper tools and a browser in app mode supply them. Short labels come from the text node of milestone 0.7 (D18).
  • Two core features decide the success. The protocol coverage lets existing tools work. The API lets plugins and agents arrange everything.

docs.title: Vision and principles
docs.text: chora is the space where forms appear.

docs.title: The name
docs.text: Plato calls the space in which things come into being chora (χώρα). chora is neither form nor matter. It only gives the forms a place. The compositor works the same way: it has no content and no policy of its own. Plugins, clients and agents bring the forms.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A desktop decides the arrangement of the content: windows, panels, workspaces. chora takes this decision out of the compositor. chora is a programmable scene. It works more like a game engine than like a window manager. The core renders a scene of nodes. One API changes the scene live.

The motivating use case is agentic interaction. The user talks to an agent, ideally by voice. The agent arranges the screen for the current task and for the taste of the user. Examples are a morning view, a data exploration view and a coding view. The agent changes the arrangement while the user works.

Agents are the motivation, not a requirement. The same scene can host a pixel-perfect Windows XP desktop, a keyboard-driven tiling setup or a KDE-like workflow. It can also host a kind of human-machine interaction that does not exist yet. chora ships none of them. chora makes all of them possible.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. Everything is a plugin. The core has no policy: no layout, no focus model, no keybindings, no decorations, no defaults. The window manager is a plugin too. A core without plugins shows a black screen.
  2. Safety is the only built-in behavior. The core keeps an escape hatch that no plugin can override: VT switch, quit, and an emergency reset. Agents will write broken code live, so this exception is necessary.
  3. Lean core, checked stability. The core stays small. Features grow in plugins, not in the core. A milestone is done only when its gate holds (D46).
  4. Reuse before writing. Wayland protocol handling, rendering, widgets, shells and services already exist. chora connects these parts and writes only what is missing. Fixes go upstream. Every decision gets a check for existing alternatives.
  5. One API for every caller. Plugins, scripts, the CLI, services and agents use the same scene language. An agent can change everything that a user can configure, and it can change it live.
  6. Live and real time. Changes apply while the session runs. They need no restart and cause no noticeable latency.
  7. Declarative and versioned. The configuration is plain text in git: views in YAML, and flavors as bundles of files. A diff shows each change. An agent can read and write the files easily.
  8. Isolation by default. Plugins run as separate processes, services in containers. Input injection and screen capture through the API need a capability that the user gives (D33).

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Reach 1.0: a daily driver on the reference hardware with a stable, versioned API (D3).
  • Run as an additional session on a Fedora host, next to the existing desktops. The concrete host is a derived secureblue image.
  • Add features as plugins and as services in containers.
  • Let a coordinator install and connect plugins and services. The first coordinator is the user. A later coordinator is an agent with special permissions that can also write new plugins and services.
  • Make it possible to rebuild any existing workflow, with effort, and to invent new ones.

docs.title: Non-goals before 1.0
docs.text:
• A usable desktop out of the box. A flavor can supply one. The core never does.
  • Agent memory and a local inventory of reusable elements. These form a separate, opinionated layer on top of chora.
  • Distributions other than Fedora, secureblue and Arch Linux (D14, D49), and NVIDIA GPUs (D11).

docs.title: chora-voice: the voice agent in Rust (draft specification)
docs.text:
Status: draft, 2026-10-30. WP0 to WP8 are done. Sources: the Python agent of before WP6 (services/voice/agent.py in git history), D53, D58, D61, D62, docs/api.md, the chora-kit runtime and settings, choractl mcp, and live probes of the Gufo servers.

chora-voice is the voice agent of chora. It completed full voice turns against the live servers in WP6; the Python agent and voice-agent.service are gone, and chora-voice.service runs it (services/voice/README.md).

docs.title: 1. Goals and non-goals
docs.text:
Goals:

  • One binary chora-voice in the crate services/voice: a chora client on the chora-kit runtime, with D62 settings.
  • Silero VAD on tract (pure Rust, no C library) as the speech gate.
  • Always listening, with the local words "Schlaf" and "Hör zu", plus the push-to-talk (PTT) key. The wake word goes through the ASR.
  • A cancel word stops the current turn at any time, also while the agent speaks or works.
  • Spoken yes/no confirmation before the tools of a configurable list.
  • Separate mute switches for the mic and the speaker.
  • No silent failure; a latency per stage for each turn; a state for the HUD.
  • Replay tests that measure speech detection and barge-in against labelled recordings.

Non-goals: new ASR, TTS or LLM servers; a keyword-spotting model; an own echo canceller (the PipeWire one stays); a GUI; a package before the agent completes full turns.

docs.title: 2. Architecture
docs.text:
One process. The core is one thread that reads one input channel. All other actors send their inputs into that channel, and the core sends effects back to them. The core holds the state machine as a pure function step(state, input) -> (state, effects), so unit tests need no IO. WP4 adds a tokio runtime for the network actors; they send into the same channel.

Actor Job audio_in A thread: the capture command at 24 kHz mono, 32 ms frames (768 samples), Silero probability and RMS per frame audio_out The playback command at 24 kHz for TTS and earcons; knows when the written sound ends; stops at once asr One websocket per utterance to Qwen3-ASR realtime, PCM in 1 s pieces tts One websocket per sentence to Qwen3-TTS, one sentence ahead llm /chat/completions with SSE and tools tools MCP client of choractl --name voice mcp, the coder tools, the confirmation gate coder One background coding task, as in Python chora A thread with the chora-kit runtime: methods, settings, PTT grab hud A thread: times the events of the HUD for the chora thread; the indicator node on its own connection NAME-hud (WP8) core State machine, speech gate, history, word matcher, turn metrics

Audio: the ASR takes 24 kHz only (WP0), and the TTS sends 24 kHz. So the mic records at 24 kHz, and the ASR gets that PCM unchanged. Only the VAD gets a 16 kHz copy: a 33-tap windowed-sinc low-pass at 7 kHz, then two samples out of each three. Subprocesses replace the pipewire crate, which needs bindgen and C headers. The commands are settings, so arecord/aplay are a fallback without code. Tests feed WAV files.

Tool layer: LLM tools go through MCP (rmcp client). The tool schemas and the plugin tools stay in one place, and chora_mcp can still run tools in a container. The agent's own needs (PTT grab, methods, settings, indicator) go through the runtime connection. This replaces the PTT polling through wait_events.

The chora thread runs runtime::run and runtime::serve of chora-kit; runtime::dispatch is public already. Methods send an input with a reply channel to the core and wait up to 1 s for the new state. When the runtime gives up after 30 s without chora, the agent exits with 1.

docs.title: 3. State machine
docs.text:
State Meaning sleeping Hears only wake words; PTT records a request listening Waits for speech recording Collects an utterance transcribing Waits for the ASR thinking Waits for the LLM, no sound tool A tool call runs confirming Waits for yes or no speaking Plays the reply working Listening while a coding task runs

The agent starts in listening (awake). The core derives the state from what goes on, in this order: an utterance in progress is recording; an utterance whose text waits is transcribing (not while asleep); a reply is confirming while a question waits, speaking while its sound plays or ran dry less than 1.5 s ago, else thinking or tool; else listening or sleeping. So speech during a reply shows as recording and transcribing, and the state of the reply comes back after it.

From Input To sleeping Short utterance with a wake word listening, earcon sleeping PTT down recording, then back to sleeping listening, working VAD onset or PTT down recording recording silence_ms quiet, PTT up, or max_turn_ms transcribing recording Less than min_speech_ms speech previous state transcribing Sleep word sleeping, earcon transcribing Cancel word, empty text or echo previous state transcribing Code cancel word previous state; the coding task stops transcribing Other text thinking thinking First sentence speaking; tools run in parallel thinking Tool call on the confirm list confirming thinking Other tool call tool tool Result or timeout thinking confirming Yes tool confirming No, two unclear answers, or timeout thinking; result "declined by the user" speaking Audio and LLM done listening or working busy states Cancel word, voice.cancel, PTT down listening, earcon any Sleep word or voice.sleep sleeping, earcon sleeping voice.wake listening, earcon

An ASR error sounds the error earcon. The final text of an older utterance still counts; a late interim text drops. An utterance while asleep only looks for a wake word; one by the PTT key is a request, and the agent sleeps again after the reply.

Barge-in while speaking: speech over the barge-in gate (section 4) for barge_in_ms pauses playback at once. The unplayed sentences stay queued. A cancel word drops them and cancels the turn. Empty text or echo plays them from the cut sentence; a spoken yes or no to a question skips the cut question. Other text ends the reply; the history keeps only the played text, and the new text starts a reply.

Speech while thinking, tool or confirming: each utterance goes to the ASR at once. A cancel word cancels. In confirming, the text is the answer. Other text waits in a queue and starts the next reply, together with the texts before it (queued in the state record). No speech is dropped. Deviation: queued text does not go into the history before the next LLM round of the running reply.

Cancel stops only the current turn: the reply task drops the SSE request and the MCP call in flight (rmcp sends notifications/cancelled), the history gets the words that played and the note "cancelled by the user; result unknown" (for a call in flight, as its tool result; for a reply whose words were all there but did not all play, in place of its words), and playback stops. A cancel word does not stop a coding task. A code cancel word ("Coding-Aufgabe abbrechen") stops it. Coding results wait for listening or working, and also go into the history.

Mute: voice.mute has two separate switches. A muted mic starts no turn by VAD, and no barge-in; PTT still records, because the key is an explicit request. A muted speaker plays no TTS and no earcons; the reply text still goes to last_reply and to the HUD.

docs.title: 4. Speech gate, echo, word matcher
docs.text:
Onset: probability over vad_threshold for onset_ms. End: under vad_release for silence_ms. An utterance keeps at most preroll_ms before the first frame of its onset. The PTT key starts an utterance at once; while the key is down, each frame counts as speech, and only the release ends the utterance.

Echo (decided in WP6, open question 4): the echo level is the level of the played sound times a coupling. The played level is the loudest RMS of the played frames in the last 160 ms (the sound reaches the mic a little later than it is written). The coupling starts at barge_in_coupling (0.1: the PipeWire echo canceller is assumed) and is learned during playback: a median tracker of mic RMS over played level (steps of 5 % per frame; only 1 % up on a frame that counts as speech). Barge-in needs probability over barge_in_vad_threshold and RMS over max(barge_in_min_rms, echo level × barge_in_echo_ratio) for barge_in_ms. Its utterance keeps that speech and preroll_ms before it: with 100 ms, the ASR heard "verbrechen" for "Abbrechen" (WP6 live). A transcript whose words match more than 80 % of the words spoken in the last 3 s is echo.

Word matcher (no LLM):

  1. Only utterances up to word_max_ms and four words count.
  2. Normalize: lowercase, no punctuation, ä→ae, ö→oe, ü→ue, ß→ss.
  3. Remove filler_words.
  4. The rest must equal a phrase. Words of four letters or more may differ by one edit; words written together also match ("Codingaufgabe").
  5. Order: code cancel, cancel, sleep, wake, yes, no. Yes and no count only in confirming.

While asleep, each short utterance goes to the ASR to find a wake word. A keyword-spotting model can replace this later.

docs.title: 5. Confirmation
docs.text: A rule matches by tool (glob), and optionally by the command kinds of apply_commands, by argv0 of run_program, or by method (glob) of call_method. The agent speaks the prompt of the rule and waits for yes or no. The method confirm answers from a key or the HUD (WP5), the spoken yes and no since WP6; two unclear answers are a no. No answer within confirm_timeout_ms is a no. A no gives the LLM the result "declined by the user; nothing happened".

docs.title: 6. Error handling
docs.text:
Component Failure Reaction Mic Capture command exits Restart, backoff 0.5 s to 5 s, error earcon once VAD Model does not load Exit 1; systemd restarts ASR Error or timeout One retry with the same audio, then earcon and phrases.asr_failed ("Ich habe dich nicht verstanden.") when the agent listens again; a wake word asleep only sounds the earcon TTS Error or timeout Earcon once per reply; the text stays in the history, in last_reply and on the HUD; the tool loop goes on; for the backoff of the TTS (1 s, doubling to 30 s), its sentences skip without a try LLM Connect error One retry, then "Das Sprachmodell antwortet nicht." LLM First token, idle or total timeout Abort, keep the rounds so far, say so LLM Context error Trim the history to half the budget, one retry LLM tool_rounds reached A final round with tool_choice: none and a note: sum up in the language of the user; without words, phrases.tool_rounds; history stays MCP Child exits Restart with backoff; call in flight gets "connection lost, result unknown"; tools reload MCP tool_timeout_s Cancel the call; result "timeout, result unknown" chora Connection closed Runtime reconnects and grabs PTT again; after 30 s, exit 1 Any thread Panic or end Exit 1; the unit has Restart=always

The history commits per LLM round; an audio failure never rolls it back. voice.health and the health of the state record show asr, tts, llm, mcp and chora as ok, down or unknown (before the first report), with the last error and its Unix time error_at. Each actor reports its successes and failures. At start, the agent warms the LLM cache, again with the backoff of the LLM until it answers, so the cache is warm when the LLM comes back. A probe connects to the websockets of the ASR and the TTS, without a request, at start, after a new URL, every 30 s, and at the end of the backoff of a server that is down. Earcons are synthesized tones: wake, sleep, cancel, error.

docs.title: 7. History and token budget
docs.text:
• context_tokens from the setting, else from the server (context_length in /v1/models; Gufo has 128000), else 32768.
  • Budget: context_tokens minus reply_reserve_tokens. The estimate counts the characters of the prompt, the tools and the messages (a picture counts as 4000), divided by the characters per token of the last request: its length over its usage.prompt_tokens (3.0 at the start; requests with a picture teach nothing). No tokenizer.
  • Before each request, drop the oldest whole turns until the estimate fits; the turn in progress stays. Before a new turn, old tool texts shrink to old_tool_chars and lose their pictures, and long arguments of old calls become {"shortened": true}; the last put_asset of each name stays whole.
  • The requests of the last saved_requests turns go to $XDG_STATE_HOME/chora/voice-history.json (default ~/.local/state), in the format of the Python agent (a list of user messages). At start, they go into the system prompt as quoted lines under "Earlier requests of the user", not as chat messages.
  • The system prompt: system_prompt, or the built-in prompt (src/prompt.md, from the Python agent); then the context_docs (FILE or FILE#HEADING for one ## HEADING section), or the built-in ones: README.md, docs/glossary.md and ten sections of docs/api.md, compiled into the binary; then prompt_file. A missing document or heading is an error at start.

docs.title: 8. ASR and TTS protocol (live probe, 2026-10-30)
docs.text:
ASR (/v1/realtime?intent=transcription, turn_detection: null):

  • The server takes only mono PCM16 at 24000 Hz. At 16000 Hz it answers invalid_audio_event: "realtime input requires mono PCM16 at 24000 Hz".
  • It sends conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.delta events only after input_audio_buffer.commit, all within about 0.4 s, then ...completed. A 3 s sentence took 0.44 s to 0.57 s after the commit.
  • So text while the user speaks needs a new transcription of the growing buffer. The setting asr_interim_ms sets the interval; 0 turns it off.

TTS (/v1/audio/speech/stream, voice aiden):

  • Per sentence: audio.start with sentence_index, sentence_text, format and sample_rate (24000), then binary PCM, then audio.done. session.done ends the session.
  • The server does not split a text: "Eins. Zwei." and a text of three sentences each came as one audio.start with sentence_index 0 (WP4 live check). So the agent splits the reply into sentences itself, one socket per sentence, as section 2 plans.
  • audio.start gives the text and the start of its sound. The HUD typewriter spreads the words of sentence_text over the PCM length of the sentence.

docs.title: 9. Settings (D62)
docs.text:
File $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/chora/chora-voice.yaml. A missing key takes its default, so an empty file is valid. settings.set applies at once (a new capture_cmd restarts capture, a new ptt_key grabs again; WP5: a new prompt warms the cache). Edits by hand apply on voice.restart. The client name is the flag --name (default voice). chora-voice --print-config prints all defaults.

Key Default asr_url ws://127.0.0.1:8881/v1/realtime?intent=transcription tts_url ws://127.0.0.1:8882/v1/audio/speech/stream llm_url http://127.0.0.1:8888/v1 model, voice gufo, aiden language, tts_language de, "" (follows language: de gives German) asr_interim_ms 0 (off) capture_cmd [pw-record, --raw, --rate, "24000", --channels, "1", --format, s16, "-"] playback_cmd [pw-play, --raw, --rate, "24000", --channels, "1", --format, s16, "-"] ptt_key Super+v vad_threshold, vad_release, onset_ms 0.5, 0.35, 96 silence_ms, min_speech_ms, max_turn_ms 800, 200, 30000 preroll_ms 300 barge_in_vad_threshold, barge_in_ms 0.7, 250 barge_in_echo_ratio, barge_in_min_rms 2.0, 300 barge_in_coupling 0.1 (start of the learned echo coupling) word_max_ms 2000 sleep_words, wake_words [schlaf, schlaf jetzt], [hör zu, hallo chora] cancel_words [stopp, stop, abbrechen, halt, vergiss es] code_cancel_words [coding-aufgabe abbrechen, programmieraufgabe abbrechen] yes_words, no_words [ja, okay, genau, mach das], [nein, nicht, lieber nicht] filler_words [bitte, jetzt, mal] confirm, confirm_timeout_ms rules below, 8000 earcons, earcon_volume true, 0.3 indicator true (state dot under screen:OUTPUT) system_prompt, context_docs "": the built-in prompt and documents prompt_file ~/.config/chora/voice-prompt.md context_tokens, reply_reserve_tokens 0 (ask the server), 1024 tool_rounds, old_tool_chars, saved_requests 10, 500, 20 reasoning_effort none asr_timeout_s, tts_timeout_s, tool_timeout_s 15, 10, 30 llm_first_token_s, llm_idle_s, llm_total_s 30, 20, 120 chora_mcp, coder_cmd [choractl], [] (no coding tools; the task is the last argument) skipped_tools (globs) [subscribe_events, wait_events, capture, "voice.*"] playback_buffer_ms 1000 phrases llm_down, llm_slow, tool_rounds, asr_failed: German sentences record_dir "" (off; else records sessions for replay)

--target NAME in capture_cmd or playback_cmd picks a PipeWire device.

confirm:
  - {tool: apply_commands, commands: [remove, close], prompt: "Soll ich das entfernen?"}
  - {tool: unload_view, prompt: "Soll ich die Ansicht entfernen?"}

docs.title: 10. Methods and events
docs.text:
Method of voice Parameters Result state none the state record below cancel, sleep, wake none the new state record mute mic: bool, speaker: bool, each optional the new state record restart none reads the settings file again settings.get, settings.set D62 D62 talk down: bool PTT from another client, for example chora-mc confirm (WP5) answer: yes\|no the new state record health (WP8) none the health record of section 6

The state record: state, since_ms (time in the state), seq (one more per change), awake, muted: {mic, speaker}, turn, last_transcript, last_reply, queued (texts that wait), coder (the parameters of agent.set for the coder, or null before the first task) and health (section 6).

HUD: the agent emits client events (D65) on its connection NAME, so a HUD subscribes to voice.* and needs no polling. The method state stays for a full state record. The indicator node signals without a HUD: with indicator, a dot of 12 pixels at the bottom right of the first output, under screen:OUTPUT, in the color of the state (input pass). The hud thread places it once per connection.

The events (D65): voice.state {state, task, said} on each change (state mapped to the states of mc: asleep, listening, thinking, working, question, speaking; task the request, said the last reply), and voice.say {state: speaking, text, duration_ms} for each sentence when its sound starts, with the length of its PCM (a late sentence gets the rest of its length). The data are the parameters of mc agent.set and mc hud.say, and chora-mc subscribes to voice.*. A coding task is a sub-agent: voice.state {name: coder, state, task, said} with state working, then done or blocked (failed or cancelled), task the task, and said its last step, then its result. The hud thread waits for the sound of a sentence and hands the events to the chora thread, which emits them on the connection of the methods: only that connection has the name voice. The chora thread looks for them every 50 ms between the events of chora. A refused event, for example over the rate limit of the core, logs at debug level.

docs.title: 11. Logging and latency
docs.text:
tracing with timestamps to stderr (journald), without colors when stderr is no terminal. RUST_LOG filters; the default is info,tract_linalg=warn. The lines are plain text in the form key=value: one call site per level in log.rs keeps the tracing macros out of the other functions, because clippy counts their expansion into the cognitive complexity. Each stage logs start and end with the turn number. One summary per turn:

turn=17 speech=2.1s asr=380ms llm_first=650ms tts_first=310ms
first_sound=1.43s tools=2/3.4s barge_ins=0 outcome=answered

first_sound (end of speech to first sound) is the main metric. WP2 logs turn, speech, length, end_wait (last speech frame to the end of the turn) and awake per utterance, for example turn=2 speech=2816ms length=3872ms end_wait=608ms awake=true, and a warning when the VAD is slower than real time. Not done: the same record in ~/.local/state/chora/voice-turns.jsonl (planned for WP8; tests/live-gate.sh reads the log instead).

docs.title: 12. Recording for replay
docs.text:
With record_dir, each run writes a directory DIR/YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS/:

  • mic.wav: all mic frames, 24 kHz, without gaps.
  • played.wav: all played sound (earcons and replies), one piece after the other.
  • events.jsonl: one line per gate event and per played piece, with the mic sample at which it happened, for example {"at": 48000, "event": "onset"} and {"at": 96000, "event": "play", "from": 0, "len": 4800}.

The WAV headers get their lengths at the end; a reader takes a cut file up to its last whole sample. chora-voice gate FILE.wav runs the speech gate of the settings over a file and prints the utterances.

For replay, a recording directory also holds labels.txt: one label per line, times in s of mic.wav, # starts a comment.

turn 1.09 2.83   # the user speaks from 1.09 s to 2.83 s
barge 2.08       # the user starts to speak over the agent

chora-voice replay DIR... runs the gates of the settings over each recording and prints the metrics of section 13. It reads the play lines of events.jsonl and, for the barge-in level, played.wav; a plain clip needs only mic.wav and labels.txt.

docs.title: 13. Test plan
docs.text:
Unit tests: every transition of step(), also cancel in each busy state; word matcher table with ASR variants and near misses ("schlafen gehen"); echo filter; sentence splitter; SSE parser; tool call deltas; confirm rules; token trimming; settings check(); the 3:2 low-pass.

Replay tests:

  • A recording: the files of section 12, plus labels.txt (turns and barge-ins). Expected words come with the word matcher (WP6).
  • The harness feeds the frames at full speed. While the agent plays, only the barge-in gate listens; a barge-in stops the playback for the rest of the recording's piece and starts an utterance with the barge-in speech and preroll_ms before it, as the agent does.
  • Metrics against the labels: missed and false turns (a detected turn matches the first unmatched labelled turn that it overlaps), onset and offset error (detected speech start and last speech frame minus the label), missed and false barge-ins (a match lies from 0.1 s before to 1 s after the label), false barge-ins per minute of agent sound, and barge-in latency. The test the_corpus_meets_the_thresholds holds them to thresholds.
  • The CI corpus is services/voice/tests/data/corpus/ (1.7 MB): hallo-chora (the clip of WP2), turns-noise, echo-barge (echo of RMS 150) and echo-loud (echo of RMS 600, WP6), the last two with played.wav. tests/corpus.py TTS_URL writes the last three again with the live TTS (user voices vivian and ryan, agent voice aiden; noise from a fixed seed): uv run tests/corpus.py ws://HOST:8882/v1/audio/speech/stream in services/voice. The TTS output changes a little from run to run, so check the metrics after a new run. Recordings from record_dir stay outside the repo.

Fake servers for CI (src/fake.rs, WP4): a scripted ASR websocket (text, error, silence, a first socket that fails), a TTS websocket (silence, 60 ms per character, one sentence per . or ?, a wrong rate, no answer); WP5 added an LLM (/models, SSE with scripted words, tool calls, HTTP errors and silence; a quarter of the request length as prompt_tokens) and an in-process MCP server for tools.rs; WP6 added an ASR with a text per utterance. With the fake tool executor, the test a_replay_runs_through_the_whole_agent (WP6) feeds recorded speech through the whole agent: a question, a cancel word over the reply, the next question. It checks the state sequence and that the second LLM request holds the played words with the cancel note.

Live tests: services/voice/tests/live.py TTS_URL ASR_URL [CLIP] checks the TTS events, the ASR at 24 kHz and 16 kHz, and writes the test clip. WP4 added the chora-voice subcommands roundtrip [TEXT] (TTS, then its sound to the ASR, with the latencies), tts TEXT [--out FILE] and asr FILE; WP3 added replay DIR...; WP5 added ask TEXT [--speak] [--yes] (one turn with the LLM and the tools of choractl mcp, with the latencies). WP6 added levels (mic level and speech probability twice a second). The URLs come from the settings. From the agent sandbox, the servers are at 192.168.178.195: ASR :8881, TTS :8882, LLM :8888 (model gufo, context 128000, text and image), reachable only with the sandbox off. The live tests also check that context_tokens: 0 reads 128000 and that describe_screen sends the picture. WP8 added services/voice/tests/live-gate.sh [TEXT]: one voice turn through the whole agent in the running chora session, against the servers of the settings, with the latency of each stage (section 15). In the agent sandbox, it ran in a headless chora session with chora-tiling.

docs.title: 14. Dependencies and packaging
docs.text:
Reused from Cargo.lock: serde, serde_json, schemars, serde-saphyr, clap, tracing, tracing-subscriber, chora-kit, chora-scene; WP4 added tokio (the workspace features and net), futures-util (sink) and base64; WP5 added rmcp (client, transport-child-process) and the tokio feature process.

New crate Why tract-onnx 0.22 Silero VAD in pure Rust. 0.23 needs Rust 1.91; the workspace has 1.89 tokio-tungstenite 0.28 (default features: no TLS; WP4) ASR and TTS websockets, fake servers reqwest 0.13 (no defaults; stream; WP5) LLM SSE; chunked HTTP by hand is a bug source. It brings hyper, tower and tower-http (MIT); 0.13 is the version of the optional rmcp dependency

tract-linalg builds its kernels with cc and needs ar at build time.

Not added: pipewire, ort, a resampler crate, a tokenizer, regex, hound, strsim. A few lines replace each.

The Silero model (MIT, LICENSES/MIT-silero-vad.txt) goes into the binary with include_bytes!. The crate lives in services/voice/ (D53) as a workspace member. No package and no unit until the agent completes full turns; since WP6, chora-voice.service replaces voice-agent.service.

docs.title: 15. Results of WP0 to WP8 (2026-10-30)
docs.text:
Silero on tract:

Model tract 0.22.5 tract 0.23.9 v5.1.2 silero_vad.onnx fails fails v4.0 silero_vad.onnx fails not tried v6.2.3 silero_vad_op18_ifless.onnx works not tried
  • v5: the export holds nested If nodes on the rate and on shapes (the LSTM squeezes an axis when it is 1). tract analyses both branches of each If, and the 8 kHz branch fails: "Attempt to squeeze an axis which dimension is not one". A fixed rate, fixed shapes or a symbolic length do not help. onnxsim and the onnxruntime optimizer cannot inline the branches either, because the branches use names from outer scopes.
  • v4: the same pattern fails at the typing step ("then" and "else" branches give different ranks).
  • v6 op18_ifless: Silero publishes this export for runtimes without If support. Only the rate check stays an If, and both of its branches analyse once the batch axis is the symbol batch. The model takes 576 samples (64 of the frame before, then 512) and a state of [2, 1, 128]. On the test clip, it finds the speech (more than 70 % of the frames over 0.5) and no speech in the quiet room. One frame takes about 5 ms in a debug build.
  • chora-voice uses v6 op18_ifless. This is not one of the two versions of the decision (v5, else v4); see open question 1.

ASR at 16 kHz: refused (section 8). The agent keeps 24 kHz end to end; only the VAD gets a 16 kHz copy.

pw-record --raw: the agent sandbox has no PipeWire and no ALSA tools, so the spike could not run them. The option -a, --raw exists in pw-cat since PipeWire 1.4.0 (not in 1.2.7). The Python agent noted that pw-record without --raw "sniffs headers and chokes on raw pipes". The capture and playback commands are settings: on a host without --raw, set them to arecord/aplay with -t raw. Tests use WAV files.

WP1 and WP2, live check in a headless chora session (a script feeds the test clip in real time as the capture command):

  • voice.state, mute, sleep, wake and settings.set answer; a wrong value answers code -32602 and changes nothing.
  • The PTT grab works, and a new ptt_key by settings.set grabs again. A key press and release within one frame (32 ms) records nothing.
  • The gate finds each pass of the clip: about 2.8 s of speech, the end 600 ms after the last speech frame with silence_ms: 600.
  • record_dir writes mic.wav, played.wav (the earcons) and events.jsonl. After a kill, the files hold everything up to the last second.

WP3, the CI corpus with the default settings (chora-voice replay):

Recording Turns Missed False Onset error Offset error Barge-ins Missed False Latency hallo-chora 1 0 0 2 ms 62 ms 0 turns-noise 2 0 0 26 ms (max 50) 50 ms (max 82) 0 echo-barge 1 0 1 160 ms 82 ms 1 0 1 416 ms
  • The fan noise (RMS 120) and the keyboard clicks start no turn; the short "Stopp." (0.48 s) is a turn.
  • Echo of RMS 150 starts no barge-in. The barge-in comes 416 ms after the first sound of the user: 256 ms of barge_in_ms plus the rise of Silero over 0.7.
  • Echo of RMS 600 without the user was a false barge-in (15 per minute of agent sound) and then a false turn: Silero gives the echo of the agent's voice a high probability, so the rule of WP3 never learned the echo level from it. WP6 takes the echo level from the played sound (section 4); see the WP6 results.
  • The harness implements the barge-in gate of section 4 (BargeIn in gate.rs) and Gate::open for the utterance that a barge-in starts. The agent uses both since WP6.

WP4, live check against the servers (chora-voice roundtrip, debug build, from the agent sandbox):

Text Audio TTS first audio TTS total ASR final after commit "Stopp." 0.56 s 466 to 472 ms 0.80 to 0.83 s 195 to 207 ms "Hallo Chora. Zeig mir bitte die Agenda für heute." 3.04 s 401 to 490 ms 4.07 s 513 to 545 ms Three sentences 6.96 s 444 ms 1309 ms echo-barge/mic.wav (asr FILE) 7.6 s 666 ms
  • The ASR heard "Hallo Cora" for "Hallo Chora" each time, and "Vardamal" for "warte mal" over echo.
  • The TTS is slower than real time for this text: 3.04 s of sound took 4.07 s. Playback that starts at the first PCM runs dry. See open question 5.
  • The time to the final text grows with the length of the utterance (0.2 s for 0.6 s, 1.3 s for 7 s). Interim texts do not shorten it: the server transcribes the whole buffer again at the commit.
  • The agent with asr_interim_ms: 1000 and a capture command that feeds echo-barge/mic.wav in real time: interim texts came every second (189 to 410 ms each), and the final text 346 to 416 ms after the end of the utterance.
  • Deviation: the TTS client takes one text per socket and reports the sentences of the server; the split into sentences and one sentence ahead come with the reply pipeline (WP5, WP6). Timeouts: the ASR has asr_timeout_s for each whole try, the TTS has tts_timeout_s for each message. "Reconnect" is a new socket per request; the ASR retries once.
  • For the HUD typewriter, tts::Event::Sentence comes before the PCM of its sentence; tts::collect gives the start and length of each sentence in samples. The HUD gets them with the speaking state (WP6) and the client events (WP8).

WP5, the LLM and the tool loop:

  • Modules: llm.rs (SSE client), tools.rs (MCP client, confirm rules), chat.rs (prompt, history, budget, tool loop), speech.rs (sentence splitter, speech with playback buffer), and the reply states in core.rs.
  • The splitter ends a sentence after .!?:; and a space, or at a line break; not after a number ("3. Oktober") or a short abbreviation ("z. B."). The first piece of a reply may end at a comma after 40 characters. It drops the marks of markdown.
  • One TTS socket per sentence, one after the other: the next sentence starts when the one before has all its sound, which is while it plays.
  • MCP: a call has tool_timeout_s; a dropped call sends notifications/cancelled (rmcp call_tool_once). A lost child answers "the connection to chora was lost; the result is unknown"; the next call or turn connects again (backoff 0.5 s to 5 s) and loads the tools again. Tools reload at the start of each turn, so new plugin methods need no restart. Dots in tool names become __ for the LLM.
  • Deviations: finish_reason: length only logs. A cancel aborts the reply task: the round in flight does not go into the history, and the note "cancelled by the user; result unknown" comes with WP6. The final round keeps the tools and sends tool_choice: none: without the tools, Gufo read the whole prompt again (21 s instead of 1.4 s).

Live check, debug build, chora-voice ask in a headless chora session with chora-tiling and one foot window, against Gufo (25 tools, prompt 22700 tokens, warm cache):

Request Tools First token Total Outcome "Welche Fenster sind gerade offen? Schau bitte nach." query_scene 1.31 s 3.6 s answered "Wie viele Fenster sind offen, und wie heißt das Layout?" (--speak) query_scene, tiling.get_layout 1.04 s 14.7 s answered "Schließ bitte das Terminal-Fenster." (confirm: no) query_scene, apply_commands declined 0.91 s 5.5 s answered Layout and plugins with tool_rounds: 1 three in one round 0.55 s 4.7 s tool_rounds The same in English three in one round 0.63 s 13.5 s tool_rounds
  • With --speak: the first sentence came 3.4 s after the request (two rounds), the TTS sent its first sound 0.56 s later, and playback started at 5.9 s, after 1 s of buffer. The TTS needs 3.2 s for the 2.4 s of "Es ist ein Fenster offen, der Terminal foot.".
  • After the declined apply_commands, the LLM said that the user declined and asked what to do. The final rounds summed up in German and in English.
  • The agent itself started in the session, connected the tools as voice-mcp, warmed the cache in 0.4 s and answered voice.confirm and voice.state; a wrong answer gives -32602.

WP6, the state machine and the first full voice turns:

  • Modules: words.rs (word matcher, echo filter), mc.rs (reports to chora-mc); the core has all states but working (WP7); speech.rs pauses and resumes the speech (Control) and reports the played PCM and each sentence with its start and length.
  • Replay with the played sound (corpus regenerated, echo-barge with one coupling for both replies, echo-loud new; the corpus cut a barge-in reply 0.8 s after the label, not 0.4 s):
Recording Turns Missed False Onset error Offset error Barge-ins Missed False Latency echo-barge 1 0 0 160 ms 82 ms 1 0 0 416 ms echo-loud 1 0 0 180 ms 70 ms 1 0 0 436 ms hallo-chora 1 0 0 2 ms 62 ms 0 turns-noise 2 0 0 26 ms (max 50) 50 ms (max 82) 0

The learned coupling is about 0.1 on echo-loud. With a start of 0.05, echo-loud has one false barge-in before the coupling grows; with 0.1 and 0.3, none. The test now wants 0 false turns and barge-ins. - Live, debug build, headless session with chora-tiling, one foot window and chora-mc, against Gufo; the mic was a script that writes a TTS clip (voice vivian) in real time, the speaker cat > /dev/null. "Welche Fenster sind gerade offen?" (2.2 s), warm cache:

Stage Time Speech end to end of the utterance 800 ms (silence_ms) ASR, final text after the commit 379 to 406 ms LLM first token (a query_scene call) 645 to 669 ms Tool query_scene 28 to 35 ms First sentence after the ASR text (two rounds) 2.4 to 2.6 s TTS first audio 408 to 424 ms First sound after the end of the utterance 4.8 to 5.0 s

first_sound holds the 1 s of playback_buffer_ms: the TTS is slower than real time. mc agent.list showed the agent voice with its task and reply; voice.state went back to listening. A cold cache (the LLM after a restart) took 40 s for the warm-up, and a turn waits for it. - Live barge-in: the clip says "Abbrechen." 8 s after the question, over the reply. The barge-in came between two sentences (the TTS ran dry), the ASR heard "Abbrechen.", the word matcher found the cancel word, and the reply stopped. Two fixes came from it: speech in a dry gap of up to 1.5 s is a barge-in, not queued text; and the barge-in utterance keeps its speech and preroll_ms (with 100 ms, the ASR heard "verbrechen"). The LLM saw the note: to the next text it said "Ich habe meine Antwort nicht zu Ende sagen können." - The TTS clips of short German phrases with tts_language: auto gave the ASR "April Rare" for "Abbrechen" and "Stopp auf Thema" for "Stopp, warte mal"; with tts_language: German it heard "Abbrechen." See open question 8.

WP7, the coder port (coder.rs):

  • The tools of the Python agent: code_task (task, optional project), code_status, code_cancel and list_projects, for the LLM only with a coder_cmd, after the tools of chora; the confirm rule of code_task asks before a task. The prompt gets the coding part of the Python agent.
  • A task clones $XDG_DATA_HOME/chora/inventory/NAME with --no-hardlinks to worktrees/NAME-N on the branch voice/N and removes origin; without a project, git init. The harness gets the task as its last argument, runs in its own process group with stdout and stderr to worktrees/NAME-N.log, and a line has at most 16 MiB. stream-json lines give the steps (tool calls and texts) and the result; other lines are steps.
  • A stop and the end of the harness end the whole process group (TERM, KILL 5 s later). code_status gives the time and the last step, or the last result; the spoken result is "The coding task in NAME-N is done|failed|was cancelled." with up to 400 characters of the result.
  • The core: working while a task runs and the agent is awake; the result waits in a queue until the state is listening or working (no utterance, no text that waits, no reply), then a reply without the LLM says it and puts it into the history as an answer. A barge-in or a cancel word stops it as any reply. The task shows in chora-mc as the agent coder.
  • Not checked live: a coding task through a spoken turn. The unit tests run sh scripts as the harness (clone without origin, log, result, cancel of a process group with a child).

WP8, error paths, health, indicator and the live gate:

  • health.rs: one record for all actors; voice.health and the state record show it. The probes and the backoffs are in section 6.
  • tts_language is empty by default and follows language (de gives German, unknown codes auto); open question 8 is decided.
  • Live, headless session: the dot voice-indicator (owner voice-hud) sat at 1256, 776 on an output of 1280x800, blue, and turned gray with voice.sleep. voice.health showed all five ok 4 s after the start; after settings.set of a tts_url without a server, tts was down with "Connection refused" within 2 s.
  • tests/live-gate.sh against Gufo, debug build, headless session with chora-tiling and no window, "Welche Fenster sind gerade offen?" (clip 2.4 s, voice vivian):
Stage First run Second run LLM warm-up 12.4 s (new prompt) 1.1 s Speech (VAD) 2.27 s 2.30 s End of speech to end of the utterance 800 ms 800 ms ASR, final text after the commit 256 ms 235 ms LLM first token 13.2 s 705 ms Tools 2 (query_scene, describe_screen), 3 rounds 1 (query_scene) 11 ms, 2 rounds TTS first audio 409 ms 196 ms First sound after the end of the utterance 16.5 s 2.7 s

In the first run, the first token came 13 s after the text, although the warm-up had ended: the request missed the cache of the server. The cause is open (the server may have served another client).

docs.title: 17. Open questions
docs.text:
1. Silero version: v5 and v4 do not load in tract (section 15); v6 op18_ifless does. Keep v6 on tract, or use ort with v5?
  2. Mic mute: is "PTT still records" correct (section 3)?
  3. pw-record --raw on the host: does the PipeWire of the host have 1.4 or later? pw-record --version shows it.
  4. Decided (WP6): the echo level comes from the played sound times a learned coupling, with a default that assumes the echo canceller. A recording with the echo canceller on the reference hardware would show the real coupling and check the default 0.1.
  5. Answered for now (WP5): playback starts after playback_buffer_ms (1 s) of sound or at the end of the sentence, and again so after it ran dry.
  6. The tools connect as NAME-mcp (voice-mcp), not as voice: the core refuses a second connection of a name with other hello flags (the runtime has resume, choractl mcp has keep_nodes). So the nodes of the LLM belong to voice-mcp, and the grant for the picture of describe_screen is choractl grant voice-mcp screen.capture. Keep this, or give choractl mcp a flag for the hello of the runtime?
  7. The built-in prompt and documents are about 22700 tokens. A cold warm-up took 41 s on Gufo; with the cache 0.2 s to 10 s. Fewer sections of docs/api.md would make a cold start faster. A turn waits for the warm-up (WP6 live: 40 s on a cold cache).
  8. Decided (WP8): tts_language follows language (de gives German); auto made the TTS clips of short German phrases hard to understand in WP6.
  9. Queued text starts the next reply; it does not go into the running reply before its next LLM round (section 3). Is that enough?
  10. first_sound is about 4.8 s after the end of an utterance with one tool call; the 1 s playback buffer and the 0.8 s silence_ms are a third of it. Lower them on the reference hardware? (WP8 live gate: 2.7 s with one short sentence.)
  11. The coder speaks its result in English ("The coding task in ... is done."), as the Python agent did, with the result of the harness in its own language. Make it a German phrase, or let the LLM sum it up (one more LLM round per task)?
  12. Decided (D65): the agent emits voice.state and voice.say, and chora-mc subscribes to voice.* (section 10). tests/voice-events.sh checks it in a headless session.
